Bitcoin price ignores Anthropic debut as ANT share price dips below $100
Bitcoin dropped toward a third retest of $62,000 as Anthropic debuted on the Nasdaq, hitting highs of $115 per share before dropping below $100.
Bitcoin shrugged off US tech-stock strength at Thursday’s Wall Street open as markets reacted to Anthropic’s $111.50 debut.
Key points:
- Anthropic opens at $111.50 per share on the Nasdaq, 34% above its IPO price of $83, rising as high as $115 before dropping to lows of $95.05.
- Bitcoin (BTC) struggled to follow equities’ upside as sell-side pressure kept BTC/USD near four-month lows of $62,000.
Anthropic debut sees share price near 40% gain versus IPO
Data from TradingView showed BTC/USD falling to $62,250 as US stock markets headed higher.
BTC/USD one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Excitement around Anthropic initially fueled 0.6% daily gains for the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index, which subsequently turned red on the day, down 1% at the time of writing. That followed 1.4% daily upside for South Korea’s tech-focused KOSPI Composite Index.
Nasdaq Composite Index one-hour chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Trading of the company’s stock on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT began at $111.50, 34% above its IPO price of $83, reaching a local high of $115 before dropping below the $100 mark amid ongoing volatility.
Anthropic shares one-minute chart. Source: Cointelegraph/TradingView
Perpetual futures traders on Hyperliquid had already placed fair value at around $103, based on a company valuation of around $1.845 trillion. Reacting, trading resource The Kobeissi Letter noted that the opening had pushed the valuation above $2 trillion, putting it in sixth place among the world’s most valuable public companies.
Previously, Cointelegraph reported on the record-breaking IPO helping to renew market trust in the AI sector amid ongoing uncertainty over Nvidia following the ousting of its CEO Jensen Huang.
“With some of the tumultuous times here for Nvidia, a little bit of that trust has gone away from the retail investor so this is the way people I think are going to express themselves,” J.J. Kinahan, senior vice president of retail and alternative investments at CBOE Global Markets, told CNBC.
In his latest analysis, economist Mohamed El-Erian called the IPO “historic.”
“On the micro side: In five years, it has gone from a startup to one of the world’s most valuable companies. It’s the largest IPO ever. On the macro side: Lots worth monitoring, starting with the flow-of-funds implications,” he summarized.

items.author: Oluwapelumi Adejumo
items.content:
Quick Take
- Threshold restored tBTC redemptions on Nov. 10 after an 11-day freeze caused by technical and security issues.
- The bridge held 4,320 BTC against 4,185 tBTC in circulation, yet holders could not redeem their tokens during the suspension.
- Threshold found no unexplained Bitcoin outflows, but the incident exposed how bridge failures can disrupt access to fully backed assets.
Threshold Network suspended tBTC redemptions for 11 days despite holding more Bitcoin than tokens in circulation.
The protocol said in a Nov. 18 post-mortem that its app stopped accepting redemption requests on Oct. 30 after unexpected bridge activity raised security concerns. Redemptions resumed Nov. 10 following technical fixes.
The interruption prevented holders from converting tBTC, a Bitcoin-backed token used across decentralized finance (DeFi), into native Bitcoin through Threshold's app. Users could still transfer and trade their existing tokens, while lending platform Aave restricted activity in its tBTC market.
However, the disruption did not appear to stem from insufficient Bitcoin reserves.
Threshold reported that its bridge wallets held 4,320.46 BTC against 4,185.155 tBTC in circulation on Oct. 31, leaving approximately 135 BTC more than the outstanding token supply.
What caused the tBTC redemption freeze?
Threshold attributed the interruption to separate technical and security issues that affected its ability to process Bitcoin transactions.
The team had identified a problem with how the bridge accounted for Bitcoin deposits before the suspension. Meanwhile, another security issue forced some node operators responsible for signing Bitcoin transactions to take their systems offline for patches.
Under Threshold's design, a bridge wallet requires signatures from more than half its designated signers to authorize a Bitcoin transaction. This meant withdrawals could not proceed until enough operators returned online.
The protocol also needed to restore Bitcoin transaction proof submissions, which allow the bridge to verify deposits and redemption payouts.
Threshold said it fixed the deposit-accounting issue and upgraded the bridge before its Council restored permission to submit Bitcoin proofs on Nov. 7.
The app subsequently reopened around 03:00 UTC on Nov. 10, allowing holders to initiate redemptions again.
The team also reviewed 57 registered tBTC wallet addresses and the bridge contracts for activity between Oct. 25 and Nov. 12.
It matched 31 BTC redemption payouts to their corresponding bridge proofs and reported finding no unexplained Bitcoin outflows in the wallets examined.
Essentially, the findings indicate the interruption was an operational failure rather than a depletion of BTC reserves.
However, the incident exposed a broader vulnerability for Bitcoin-backed assets used in DeFi: even when reserves are sufficient, technical failures can temporarily prevent holders from accessing their underlying BTC.
items.title: Threshold’s 11-day Bitcoin redemption freeze exposes a hidden risk in BTC-backed tokens

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Four people were arrested outside Nasdaq’s Times Square headquarters during Anthropic’s IPO celebrations, according to protest organizers and news reports.
- Activists warned that faster stock-index inclusion could expose pension and 401(k) savers to volatile AI shares, though no rule forces every fund to buy the IPO.
- The demonstration also targeted AI’s impact on jobs, data centers, surveillance and military operations.
At least four protesters have been arrested outside Nasdaq’s Times Square headquarters Thursday as Anthropic celebrated its $81.34 billion initial public offering, according to a press release shared with Decrypt by organizers of the #StopTechOligarchs demonstration.
The Stop Funding Billionaires campaign accused Anthropic and its early investors of benefiting from an AI boom that could leave ordinary retirement savers exposed if share prices tumble. Organizers called on pension funds and other large investors to stay away from the company's stock.
“Teachers, firefighters, civil servants will pay for that loss,” said Jose Gonzalez, an activist with Stop Funding Billionaires and New York Communities for Change, in a statement. He argued that workers have little control over how large institutions invest the savings they depend on for retirement.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
The concern centers on faster rules for adding new companies to major stock indexes. Under Nasdaq’s fast-entry policy, an eligible IPO large enough to rank among the Nasdaq-100’s top 40 companies can enter the index after 15 trading days, allowing index-tracking funds to buy the shares sooner than under older rules.
That does not mean all pension funds or 401(k) plans must purchase Anthropic shares, let alone buy them during the IPO. Funds tracking a benchmark that admits Anthropic would normally adjust their holdings, while other managers can make different choices.
Protesters also raised concerns about AI-driven job displacement, the water and energy used by data centers, and AI applications in surveillance and military targeting. Their claims about specific military and law-enforcement harms were allegations made by the campaign, not findings established by the release.
“I’m proud to join activists and community members out here today to stand against Anthropic and the tech billionaires who put profit over people,” said New York state senator-elect Aber Kawas in the organizers’ statement. Kawas also criticized AI’s military uses and the prospect of companies replacing workers with automated systems.
One protester identified by organizers as among those arrested called for a freeze on what they described as reckless AI development. “Don’t bail out Big Tech when their bubble inevitably pops,” the protester said.
Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83 apiece, raising $81.34 billion in the initial offering. That exceeded SpaceX’s original $75 billion IPO sale, although SpaceX’s final offering was larger after underwriters bought additional shares.
The IPO also followed a sharp change in market expectations. Earlier this month, an AI-stock sell-off had led some investors to question whether Anthropic could command a valuation above $1 trillion, before demand pushed its IPO price higher.
The protesters had called for Anthropic to halt its IPO, even as the offering went ahead. The campaign is also urging pension funds, university endowments and other institutional investors not to buy shares in companies it says undermine workers’ rights.

Quick Take
- Arthur Hayes set four crypto price targets less than a month after saying he closed Maelstrom’s directional book.
- Zcash needed a 97.3% gain from its Nov. 18 Coinbase close to hit Hayes’s target, the largest gap of the four.
- Hayes described low conviction and gave no deadline or details of any purchases by him or Maelstrom.
Arthur Hayes has just set bullish price targets for Ethereum, Zcash, NEAR and Venice Token, less than a month after saying he closed Maelstrom’s directional trading book. His $1,800 Zcash target was 97.3% above the token’s Nov. 18.
In a Nov. 17 post, Hayes called the tokens his “Four Horsemen.” He put ETH at $2,800, ZEC at $1,800, NEAR at $6 and VVV at $40. He described the prospective trade size as “small to medium,” expressed little conviction and expected a rally before the end of what he called the AI bubble.
The post gave no deadline for the targets. Hayes gave no details about purchases by him or Maelstrom, or about the fund’s current exposure.
What Hayes said about Maelstrom’s trading
On Oct. 24, CryptoSlate reported that Hayes said he had closed Maelstrom’s directional book and taken profits on ETH, Ethena, Uniswap and other tokens. The exit covered bets on which way prices would move. ETH was among the tokens he sold and one of the four he expects to rally.
Hayes set out his condition for staying on the sidelines in a Nov. 5 essay. He wrote that Maelstrom would wait unless the fiat liquidity picture changed dramatically. His concern was that a decline in AI stocks could make lenders demand higher yields from those companies. That would make debt harder to issue and, in his view, leave less dollar liquidity available to markets.
NEAR and ZEC were names Hayes had publicly walked away from before. In a June 8 essay, he wrote that he had sold NEAR the previous week and gave a separate reason for exiting ZEC, citing a bug in Zcash’s Orchard privacy pool. The two tokens are now back in his public outlook, and ZEC has the widest gap to its target.
How far prices were from Hayes’s targets
Three of the four tokens lost ground between the Nov. 17 and Nov. 18 UTC closes on Coinbase Exchange. ZEC fell the most, down 5.6%, and VVV was the only gainer, up 2.8%. The figures compare two complete daily candles for the exchange’s USD pairs, with each date marking the start of its UTC trading day.
| Token | Nov. 17 close | Nov. 18 close | Daily change | Hayes’s target | Rise to target | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETH | $1,822 | $1,775 | −2.6% | $2,800 | 57.8% | 
| ZEC | $967 | $912 | −5.6% | $1,800 | 97.3% | 
| NEAR | $3.39 | $3.3 | −2.8% | $6 | 81.9% | 
| VVV | $21.07 | $21.67 | +2.8% | $40 | 84.6% | 
The percentage columns use the unrounded closes.
Hayes’s $40 target for Venice Token would also top the Sept. 21 record listed on CryptoSlate’s Venice Token market page.

items.author: Decrypt Agent
items.content:
In brief
- Perpetual futures, or perps, are derivatives contracts that track an asset's price but, unlike traditional futures, never expire.
- A mechanism called the funding rate keeps a perp's price close to the underlying asset, with traders on one side periodically paying those on the other.
- Perps let traders use leverage to go long or short, but leveraged positions can be wiped out quickly through liquidation.
Perpetual futures are the engine room of crypto trading. Centralized exchanges processed $85.3 trillion in perps trading volume in 2025 alone, according to CoinGecko's State of Crypto Perpetuals Report 2026, and the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) describes perps as the dominant form of crypto derivatives trading.
They aren't only for crypto, either. Exchanges now offer perps on stocks, commodities and currencies, and Decrypt has become the first news publisher to offer perps trading, powered by Solana exchange Phoenix.
This guide explains what futures are, what makes perpetual futures different, how funding rates and liquidations work, and what to know before trading them.
What are futures?
To understand perpetual futures, it helps to start with ordinary futures.
A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an asset at a set price on a set date in the future. Futures have been used for centuries: farmers used them to lock in prices for crops before harvest, and today they are traded on everything from oil and wheat to stock indexes and Bitcoin, on regulated exchanges such as CME.
Traders use futures for two main reasons. Hedgers use them to protect against price swings; an airline might buy oil futures to lock in fuel costs, for example. Speculators use them to bet on price movements without owning the underlying asset.
Traditional futures have an expiry date. When a contract expires, it settles, either by delivering the asset or, more often, by paying out the difference in cash. Traders who want to keep their position open must "roll" it into a new contract, which can add costs and complexity.
What makes perpetual futures different?
Perpetual futures, often shortened to "perps" or "perpetual swaps," work like futures, but with one key difference: they never expire. Traders can hold a position for as long as they like, provided they have enough collateral to keep it open.
The idea was proposed by Yale economist Robert Shiller in a 1993 paper as a way to create markets for assets that are hard to trade directly. Perps took off in crypto. Crypto exchange BitMEX, widely credited with bringing perps to crypto, launched a perpetual contract on Bitcoin in 2016. BitMEX itself closed in September 2026, but the product it pioneered has become the most traded instrument in crypto.
Did you know?
A perpetual contract never actually involves owning the asset. Traders deposit collateral, or "margin," and their profit or loss depends entirely on how the price moves.
How do perpetual futures work?
When opening a perp position, a trader chooses a direction. Going long means betting the price will rise; going short means betting it will fall. Being able to short as easily as going long is one reason perps are popular: it lets traders profit from falling prices, or hedge assets they already own.
Perps are usually traded with leverage, which lets traders control a larger position than their collateral alone would allow. With 10x leverage, for example, $100 of margin controls a $1,000 position. If the asset's price rises 5%, the trader makes $50, a 50% return on their margin. But if it falls 5%, they lose $50, half of their margin.
Exchanges track two prices to manage this. The index price is the asset's price on spot markets, usually averaged across several exchanges. The mark price, based on the index and the perp market itself, is used to calculate profits and losses and to decide when positions must be closed. Using an averaged price makes it harder for a sudden spike on one exchange to trigger liquidations.
What is the funding rate?
Because perps never expire, nothing forces their price to converge with the underlying asset, as traditional futures do at expiry. Instead, perps use a funding rate.
At regular intervals—most commonly every eight hours, though some platforms use shorter or longer schedules—traders on one side of the market pay traders on the other:
- When the perp trades above the index price, the funding rate is positive, and longs pay shorts. That makes it more expensive to be long, encouraging traders to sell and pushing the perp price down toward the index.
- When the perp trades below the index price, the funding rate is negative, and shorts pay longs, pulling the price back up.
Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid, for example, pays funding every hour, at one-eighth of the rate calculated for an eight-hour period, to stay consistent with centralized exchanges.
Funding payments go directly between traders, not to the exchange. For traders holding positions over long periods, these payments can add up, and they can either boost or erode returns.
Funding rates also offer a window into market sentiment. Strongly positive funding suggests traders are crowded into bullish bets, while negative funding shows that bears are paying to stay short.
Rates for the same asset can also differ between exchanges. On November 19, 2026, Bitcoin's funding rate was 0.01% per eight hours on Hyperliquid, compared with 0.0037% on Binance, according to Hyperliquid's funding comparison tool.
Did you know?
Some traders aim to earn funding payments rather than bet on prices. In a "cash and carry" or basis trade, they buy an asset on the spot market and short the same amount through perps, collecting funding while their positions offset each other's price moves.
What is liquidation?
Leverage is a double-edged sword. Every perp position has a maintenance margin, the minimum collateral needed to keep it open. If losses push a trader's margin below that level, the exchange automatically closes the position, a process called liquidation. The trader typically loses most or all of the margin they put up.
The higher the leverage, the smaller the price move needed to trigger a liquidation. At 50x leverage, a 2% move against a position can wipe it out.
Liquidations can also feed on each other. When prices fall sharply, liquidated longs are forced to sell, pushing prices lower and triggering further liquidations, a so-called liquidation cascade. On October 10, 2025, the crypto market saw its largest liquidation event on record, with more than $19 billion in leveraged positions wiped out in a single day.
To cover losses when positions can't be closed in time, exchanges typically keep an insurance fund. In extreme cases, some use auto-deleveraging, closing profitable positions on the other side of the market to keep the system solvent.
Crypto perps: centralized and decentralized
Crypto perps trade on two main types of venue.
Centralized exchanges, such as Binance, Bybit and OKX, run their own order books and hold users' funds. They account for the vast majority of perps trading: Binance alone held about a third of centralized perps volume in early 2026, according to CoinGecko. Many are unavailable to U.S. customers.
Decentralized exchanges let traders use perps through smart contracts, while keeping control of their funds. Some, such as Hyperliquid and Solana-based Phoenix, run order books onchain, matching buyers and sellers much like a traditional exchange. Others, such as GMX and Jupiter, let traders trade against a shared pool of liquidity provided by other users.
Decentralized perps are growing fast. Their trading volume jumped from $1.5 trillion in 2024 to $6.38 trillion in 2025, led by Hyperliquid, CoinGecko found. Decentralized exchanges' share of perps trading volume peaked at 13% in late 2025 before slipping to 10% in April 2026, while their share of open interest, the total value of open positions, reached 13.5%.
In the U.S., perps developed largely on offshore exchanges, outside the reach of the CFTC, but that has started to change. In July 2025, Coinbase introduced CFTC-regulated "perpetual-style" futures for U.S. customers, with five-year expiries and up to 10x leverage. Two months later, CFTC-regulated exchange Bitnomial launched what it called the first U.S. perpetual futures, with 25-year terms and eight-hour funding. In May 2026, the CFTC approved a Bitcoin perpetual futures contract from prediction market Kalshi and set out a framework for listing more, and in June, Kraken rolled out perps to eligible U.S. customers through Bitnomial, which its parent company had acquired.
Some of these contracts, including Kalshi's and Bitnomial's original design, have long but fixed terms of 25 years, so are not strictly perpetual. The regulator says perps can be offered on CFTC-registered exchanges under federal oversight, and has advised U.S. traders to avoid offshore venues.
The shift has been contested. CME Group, the largest U.S. futures exchange, has sued the CFTC, arguing that perps are swaps rather than futures under U.S. law. The CFTC has nonetheless continued to approve more perps platforms, starting with Backpack.
Beyond crypto
Perps are now spreading beyond crypto. Exchanges have begun listing perps tracking stocks, stock indexes, commodities such as gold and oil, and currencies, giving traders around-the-clock exposure to markets that normally close in the evening and on weekends.
Those products carry the same mechanics, and the same risks, as crypto perps. They track an asset's price without giving traders ownership of the asset itself, so a perp on a company's stock doesn't come with voting rights or dividends.
What are the risks?
Perps can be useful tools for hedging and speculation, but they are among the riskiest products in crypto:
- Leverage magnifies losses as well as gains, and liquidation can wipe out a position in minutes.
- Funding costs can erode returns on positions held for long periods.
- Volatility in crypto markets means prices can move sharply in a short time, especially during liquidation cascades.
- Platform risk matters too: centralized exchanges can be hacked or fail, and decentralized ones can suffer smart contract bugs or oracle failures.
How to trade perps on Decrypt
Decrypt users can now trade perps directly alongside the news, through the Decrypt Money Account. The service is powered by Phoenix, a decentralized exchange on Solana, and lets users go long or short on crypto, stocks and commodities.
Availability varies by region, and as with any leveraged product, traders should only risk money they can afford to lose.

Decrypt offers perpetual futures trading through the Decrypt Money Account, powered by Phoenix.

Ledger CTO Charles Guillemet is stepping down from the company at the end of this year to devote his time to “solving this security mess.”
Guillemet announced his resignation on X today, bringing to an end 10 years with the hardware wallet firm.
He noted his work in building Donjon, Ledger’s cybersecurity team, crypto’s transformation from a niche product to modern finance infrastructure, and AI’s ability to make “attacks cheaper, faster and easier to scale.”
Guillemet posted, “The question we spent a decade answering for crypto (how do you protect what matters when any device can be compromised?) is now a question for every company, every AI agent and every government”
He now claims he is moving on to build something new and that he will dedicate his time “to solving this security mess. More very soon.”
Ledger CTO leaves one security mess to solve another
Instances of spyware discovered in Ledger wallets have recently spread from its official Malaysian resellers to resellers across Dubai and Germany.
Crypto sleuth ZachXBT now estimates that spyware has drained over $105 million from victims and asked Ledger, “So who will be covering all of the losses?”
Ledger has also been grappling with multiple third-party data breaches over the years that have led to the leaking of customer data and lawsuits.

In brief
- Anthropic shares are indicated to open at $110, approximately 33% above their $83 IPO price.
- The implied fully diluted valuation is approaching $2 trillion.
- AI-linked stocks rallied Thursday as Anthropic's founders rang the Nasdaq opening bell.
Anthropic shares opened at $111.50 on Thursday, approximately 33% above their $83 initial public offering price, as investors piled into the Claude developer on its highly anticipated Nasdaq debut.
Initial indications on the IPO open climbed from $108 earlier in the session, with successive price estimates reportedly moving closer together, Yahoo reported.
During the opening process, market makers and underwriters monitor incoming buy and sell orders to determine a price at which supply and demand can meet. Indications quickly climbed as Nasdaq established its official opening price.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.
At $111, Anthropic commands a fully diluted valuation approaching $2 trillion, up from around $1.5 trillion at its IPO price. That represents nearly $500 billion in additional implied market value before its first public trade.
The excitement is spreading beyond Anthropic itself. U.S. stocks climbed Thursday, with semiconductor companies leading a broader rally in AI-related shares. Optical equipment makers, laser technology firms and neocloud providers also advanced, helping lift the technology sector as investors awaited Anthropic's first trade.
At the Nasdaq ceremony, Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei rang the opening bell, marking a milestone for one of the world's most prominent AI developers.
Daniela, who serves as the company's president, used the occasion to address people concerned about AI's growing influence.
"This technology needs you. Not your trust, not your use, but your voice," she said, urging the public to participate in shaping the technology's future.
"The end of the story isn't written yet. Intelligence is now something humans can build. What we choose to build with it is up to all of us," she added.
Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83, raising $81.34 billion—more than SpaceX's initial $75 billion IPO, although still below its expanded final offering.
The debut follows a remarkable turnaround in sentiment. Just two weeks ago, some major investors were questioning whether Anthropic could sustain a $1.5 trillion valuation, with one suggesting it might need to accept something closer to $1 trillion.
For investors allocated shares at $83, a $110 opening translates into an immediate paper gain of $27 per share.
The bigger question is whether Anthropic's strong debut marks renewed confidence in the AI boom—or simply another example of investors paying increasingly extraordinary prices for its biggest names.

SEC 指控，被告通过伪造 SEC 证书、向 SEC、美国金融业监管局（FINRA）或金融犯罪执法网络（FinCEN）提交备案，并将持怀疑态度的投资者引导至相关证书和文件，以营造合法假象。

items.author: Oluwapelumi Adejumo
items.content:
Quick Take
- Bitwise filed for a Zcash ETF that would allow direct ZEC redemptions, challenging Grayscale's existing $489 million fund.
- The proposed structure could lower trading costs and improve ETF pricing as Bitwise CIO Matt Hougan predicts a potential Bitcoin-to-Zcash rotation.
- Bitwise's ETF will avoid shielded transactions, while exchange restrictions and looming EU rules threaten Zcash's institutional ambitions.
Bitwise is seeking to challenge Grayscale's Zcash ETF with a structure that would give Wall Street firms greater flexibility in trading the privacy-focused cryptocurrency.
The asset manager's Nov. 17 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) proposes allowing authorized participants to redeem ETF shares directly for ZEC or receive cash, unlike Grayscale's existing Zcash ETF, which currently permits only cash redemptions.
The proposed fund would trade on the Texas Stock Exchange under the ticker ZEC, expanding competition in a market where Grayscale's ZCSH has traded on NYSE Arca since August.
Grayscale's fund recently held approximately $489 million in assets, while its September quarterly report disclosed $50.5 million in gross redemptions during the preceding three months.
The difference in redemption structures could influence trading costs and how closely the competing funds track the value of their underlying ZEC holdings.
How Bitwise's redemption model differs from Grayscale
Under Bitwise's proposal, authorized participants could return blocks of 10,000 ETF shares to the fund and receive the corresponding amount of ZEC.
That would give professional trading firms greater control over how they sell or hedge the cryptocurrency, potentially allowing them to capture differences between the ETF's market price and the value of its holdings.
For instance, when ETF shares trade below their net asset value, a firm could purchase discounted shares, redeem them for ZEC, and sell the coins at a higher combined value after accounting for costs.
Such transactions can help narrow the discount between ETF shares and their underlying assets.
Grayscale's existing structure also supports arbitrage, but introduces another intermediary into the redemption process.
Its prospectus requires authorized participants to receive cash, while a liquidity provider delivers the money and receives ZEC from the fund.
Depending on the order arrangement, the liquidity provider or authorized participant bears the difference between the fund's calculated value and the actual price obtained when disposing of the coins.
Bitwise's approach would allow participating firms to manage that execution themselves, potentially reducing costs when they can access sufficient liquidity.
The proposed flexibility also extends to creating new shares, with Bitwise allowing authorized firms to deliver ZEC or cash.
However, the approach would place greater importance on the firms' ability to trade ZEC efficiently, particularly during periods of heightened volatility.
Bitwise's Zcash privacy thesis faces regulatory restrictions
The filing follows comments from Bitwise chief investment officer Matt Hougan, who sees growing demand for financial privacy as traditional institutions deepen their involvement in cryptocurrency markets.
In a November interview, Hougan argued that Zcash has become increasingly differentiated from Bitcoin as institutional adoption accelerates.
He suggested that longtime cryptocurrency investors could eventually rotate some Bitcoin holdings into privacy-focused assets as institutions absorb more of the flagship cryptocurrency's supply.
Hougan also described Zcash as occupying a distinctive position between Bitcoin and Monero, combining institutional compatibility with privacy functionality. He said:
“I'm bullish on the privacy thesis.”
That investment thesis presents an interesting distinction in Bitwise's proposed fund.
Although Zcash supports shielded transactions that conceal certain transaction details using zero-knowledge cryptography, the ETF itself would not use those features.
The filing also acknowledges that Zcash's privacy functionality has created regulatory obstacles.
Several cryptocurrency exchanges have delisted or restricted ZEC over compliance concerns, while some platforms that continue supporting the asset permit transactions only through transparent addresses.
Bitwise identified restrictions affecting Zcash trading on exchanges including OKX and Binance, warning that reduced market access could affect prices and liquidity.
The filing also highlighted European Union anti-money laundering rules taking effect in July 2027 that will prohibit regulated financial providers from maintaining accounts that enable transaction anonymization.
The rules' application to cryptocurrencies supporting both transparent and shielded transactions remains uncertain, leaving Zcash's institutional ambitions exposed to further regulatory scrutiny.
items.title: Bitwise challenges Grayscale’s $489 million Zcash ETF as CIO predicts Bitcoin-to-ZEC rotation

Anthropic shares open at $111.50, 34.3% above $83 IPO price
The Claude chatbot maker began trading under the ticker ANT, with the company’s valuation at around $2 trillion at the opening price.
Anthropic shares opened trading under the ticker ANT on the Nasdaq at $111.50 Thursday, about 34.3% above their initial public offering (IPO) price.
The Wall Street Journal had reported an expected opening of $110 minutes before trading began as fresh headlines poured in by the minute with ever-rising opening price predictions. The opening price values Anthropic at around $2 trillion on a fully diluted basis.
Anthropic had priced 980 million shares at $83 on Wednesday, above its initial $70-$78 range. The $81.3 billion IPO includes stock from existing shareholders. A separate $26 billion private placement brings the combined deal to $107.3 billion.
Anthropic’s IPO has blasted past SpaceX’s record $75 billion IPO in June, showing that the scale of investor demand for AI companies appears undeterred. SpaceX shares opened at $150, above their $135 offer price.
Source: Renaissance Capital/Reuters
Crypto exchange OKX said in a note shared with Cointelegraph that its Anthropic pre-IPO perpetual contract traded at about 103 USDC (USDC) earlier Thursday, roughly 24% above the offer price. The contract provides derivative exposure without ownership of Anthropic shares. Binance Wallet and Kraken also offered eligible users tokenized IPO exposure through xStocks. However, both warned that actual allocations could be partial or even zero, with unused funds returned.
Crypto platforms also offered exposure ahead of SpaceX’s listing, although Binance, Bybit, Bitget Wallet and MEXC later canceled their tokenized IPO campaigns after failing to secure share allocations.
Anthropic faces stiff competition from OpenAI and DeepSeek while committing billions to computing infrastructure, including a $28 billion, 15-year data center lease with Bitcoin miner Riot Platforms. Anthropic has committed around $901 billion in total to purchases and leases, mostly for computing power and infrastructure, according to its IPO filing, with spending stretching out as far as 2045.
Cointelegraph reported earlier Thursday that Bitcoin rebounded from $62,000 as US stock futures rose ahead of Anthropic’s public debut.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83, raising $81.34 billion—above SpaceX's $75 billion initial offering but below its $86.25 billion expanded IPO.
- Google, Nvidia, and five other companies committed a separate $26 billion. Together with the new IPO shares, Anthropic expects $104.8 billion in net proceeds after fees.
- Behind the deal: explosive customer spending, $900.9 billion in infrastructure commitments and an OpenAI IPO potentially coming in 2027.
Anthropic has priced the largest initial IPO share sale in history at $81.34 billion, topping the $75 billion SpaceX first sold in June. But SpaceX still has the larger completed IPO after an additional share sale.
The Claude maker sold 980 million shares at $83 on Wednesday and is set to begin trading Thursday on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.
The price beat the original $70-to-$78 range, while the company increased the offering from 825 million shares. Demand was about six times the number available before pricing.
Did you know?
You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perps on Decrypt.
At $83, Anthropic is valued at roughly $1.5 trillion including stock options and other potential shares, though its value based on outstanding shares is closer to $1.1 trillion.
Where the $107 billion goes
The headline $81.34 billion isn't all money for Anthropic. About 956.35 million new shares bring $79.38 billion into the company before fees. Another 23.65 million shares, worth $1.96 billion, are being sold by its seven co-founders—roughly $280 million each. Anthropic receives none of that founders' cash, according to its final prospectus.
On top of the public sale, seven technology companies are buying $26 billion of nonvoting stock in a separate private placement. Google and Nvidia are putting in $10 billion each, AMD $2.5 billion, Broadcom, Micron and Microsoft $1 billion each, and TSMC $500 million.
The public offering and private placement total $107.34 billion in gross share sales, including the $1.96 billion going to founders rather than Anthropic.
The $104.8 billion net figure is for both transactions, not for the IPO alone. Anthropic gets $79.38 billion from its newly issued public shares, plus $26 billion from the private placement: $105.38 billion before costs. Subtract roughly $580 million in company-paid underwriting fees and estimated offering expenses, and the prospectus estimates $104.8 billion net.
That said, it could rise to about $117 billion if underwriters buy all the extra shares allowed. Anthropic plans to spend the money on operations, hiring and, above all, computing infrastructure.
Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led a 22-bank underwriting group, with roughly $550 million in underwriting commissions. The company also offered access through brokers including Fidelity, Schwab, Robinhood, and SoFi, but retail investors received less than 20% of the offering.
The winners—and who still controls Anthropic
Amazon remains the largest disclosed shareholder after the transaction with about 14.6% of the company, followed by Google at roughly 13.4%.
Early financial backers also hold enormous paper fortunes. Bloomberg estimates put Lightspeed's stake near $28 billion, Iconiq's above $26 billion and Menlo Ventures' around $22 billion. Ashton Kutcher's Sound Ventures reportedly holds shares worth almost $11 billion. Those figures are estimates of stock value, not cash they received at the IPO.
Investors, however, aren't buying much control. A special share class gives the founders' holding company 50.1% of shareholder voting power, while the Long-Term Benefit Trust can appoint a majority of the board.
So, Anthropic can raise historic sums while keeping key decisions largely away from ordinary shareholders.
The business growing almost too fast to measure
Anthropic generated $33.24 billion in revenue during the first nine months of 2026, including $16.96 billion in the third quarter alone—the latest reported quarter. Its $81 billion annualized revenue run rate at the end of October projects recent customer spending over a year; it isn't money already earned.
Roughly 250 organizations now spend at least $10 million annually with Anthropic, and more than 1,900 spend at least $1 million, using trailing 12-month figures. Its net revenue retention reached about 900%.
In plain English, the same eligible customer group spent nine times as much in the latest three-month period as it did a year earlier. That measure excludes fixed-price Claude subscriptions.
But the business still depends on a few major accounts and distribution partners. Its five biggest customers generated about 25% of revenue over the first nine months of 2026, while cloud marketplaces accounted for 44%. In other words, companies like Amazon, Google and Microsoft can invest in Anthropic, provide the machines it runs on and help sell access to Claude.
Even the product changes at extraordinary speed: Claude models released during the six months through September made up more than 80% of third-quarter revenue. At the end of September 2026, Anthropic had about 5,300 employees and was generating more than $6.6 million in trailing annual revenue per employee.
An enormous business with an even bigger bill
Rapid growth doesn't mean easy profits. Anthropic posted a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter of 2026, after a $974 million operating profit in the second quarter. Over the first nine months, its operating loss totaled $1.26 billion. Those numbers tell a very different story from its much bigger headline net loss.
In the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic posted a $104.04 billion net loss, including $94.3 billion in noncash revaluations of convertible financing and related instruments. Yet it generated $6.57 billion in cash from operating activities during the same period. That is not free cash flow, which also accounts for capital spending, but the distinction matters: a $104 billion accounting loss does not mean $104 billion of cash burned.
The latest balance sheet, dated September 30, 2026, shows $95.6 billion in cash and equivalents plus $36.3 billion in short-term investments—$131.85 billion combined. Convertible notes payable stood at $130.50 billion at their accounting value, with some converting into shares around the IPO.
The final prospectus estimates $232.35 billion in cash and short-term investments on a pro forma, post-transaction basis. That last figure is a modeled balance after the offering and related adjustments, not cash the company held on September 30.
The more consequential number may be what it has promised to spend next. Anthropic disclosed about $900.9 billion in commitments, overwhelmingly for computing and infrastructure, stretching as far as 2045.
It separately estimates another $150 billion to $175 billion in payments under arrangements without fixed dollar amounts. Together, that points to potentially more than $1 trillion—but it is not a bill due today, and some contracts are conditional or can be terminated.
Some $70.7 billion of the stated commitments fall due in the 12 months after September 2026. That explains why even an IPO this large is not necessarily excessive capital for a frontier AI company. Every breakthrough attracts customers, but serving them requires more chips, power, and data centers.
What the SpaceX record means for OpenAI
There is a technical catch to the record. SpaceX's June IPO initially sold $75 billion in shares, but the final deal reached $86.25 billion gross after underwriters bought more shares—about $85.675 billion after fees, according to SpaceX's SEC filing.
Anthropic's $81.34 billion beats SpaceX's initial deal, not its final gross total. The extra $26 billion from Anthropic's private placement cannot be counted as public IPO proceeds. Its own option covers another 147 million shares worth about $12.2 billion; if exercised in full, its public IPO would reach $93.54 billion, comfortably above SpaceX's final figure.
Now attention turns to OpenAI. The ChatGPT maker recently raised $11 billion at a reported $1.25 trillion valuation and has indicated it will not list before 2027. Anthropic's debut offers a public-market test of what investors are willing to pay for AI revenue, while exposing the cost of generating it.
The interesting part isn't just that a five-year-old AI lab topped SpaceX's initial IPO. It's that it assembled more than $100 billion in combined public and private financing, started generating cash from operations—and still faces a potential trillion-dollar computing bill.

Anthropic IPO料造就数百名亿美元富豪，员工人均持股价值约4400万美元

动察 Beating AI 快讯，据《财富》报道，按 Anthropic 每股 83 美元的 IPO 发行价计算，公司 5300 名员工合计持有的股权估值约为 2320 亿美元，折合人均约 4400 万美元。

至少 400 名早期员工的身家将达到 1 亿美元或以上，其中部分人可能加入公司七名联合创始人的行列，成为亿万富豪。非创始人员工在首个交易日最多可出售个人持股的 10%，公司公布 2026 年业绩后，另有 35% 的个人持股将获得出售资格。

此次 IPO 对 Anthropic 的估值为 1.5 万亿美元，按上市估值衡量，规模位居历史第二，仅次于 SpaceX 的 1.77 万亿美元。不过，按募资额计算，Anthropic 的 810 亿美元超过了 SpaceX 的 750 亿美元。

七名联合创始人的持股比例相对均衡，预计每人的身家将大致翻倍至约 199 亿美元。七人均已承诺将个人所持 Anthropic 股权的 80% 用于慈善事业，相关承诺对应的价值可能超过 1000 亿美元。

与此同时，CEO Dario Amodei 曾在今年 1 月发表的文章中警告，AI 带来的巨额财富可能集中到足以破坏社会的程度。他将 AI 热潮与美国镀金时代相比较，认为处于 AI 经济繁荣前沿的人，应愿意放弃部分财富与权力，并向社会回馈。

items.author: Liam 'Akiba' Wright
items.content:
Quick Take
- The Nov. 18 census linked 7.16 million BTC to public keys or scripts already on-chain, equal to 35.6% of unspent bitcoin at block 975,019.
- About 73% of the tally came from historical matches, including roughly 1.93 million BTC in script-hash formats.
- Planning a future quantum migration would require checking which spending paths depend on public keys that are already visible.
A Bitcoin census published Nov. 18 linked 7.16 million unspent BTC to public keys or scripts already visible on-chain. It counted some outputs because they contain key data by design and others because their hashes matched tables built from earlier on-chain data. Together they accounted for 35.6% of the BTC in unspent outputs at block 975,019.
Researcher duncan0k published the census on Delving Bitcoin, tallying 7,164,754 BTC out of 20,109,207 BTC in unspent outputs. About 1.94 million BTC qualified by format alone, across pay-to-public-key, Taproot and bare multisig outputs. Those formats put key data in the output itself. The census counted them in full, including a small amount in outputs that failed its key validity check.
The other 5.23 million BTC, about 73% of the tally, came from matching hashes in unspent outputs to older blockchain data. About 3.30 million BTC of that sat in two formats that use a hash of a public key. Another 1.93 million BTC sat in two script-hash formats, which record a fingerprint of the instructions for spending the coins.
What the Bitcoin census counts as a script match
A script-hash match is a clue to how the coins can be spent. When it identifies a revealed script, a reviewer can check which signatures a spending path requires and whether the corresponding public keys are already visible. Some paths require no signature at all. Those distinctions matter if future quantum computers become capable of breaking the signatures Bitcoin uses today.
The extraction rules describe two ways the scan counted script-hash balances. A pay-to-script-hash output can match a previously revealed script or an entry derived from a known public key. The other script-hash format uses a separate table that also includes some hashes derived from Taproot script data.
The researcher compared those rules with draft BIP 362, a proposal to classify exposure in existing Bitcoin outputs. Compared with the draft version reviewed, the scan skipped some revealed scripts and included some broader matches. The net effect is unmeasured. Keys or scripts behind outputs outside the tally could still have been disclosed off-chain or in on-chain locations the scan skipped.
Glassnode’s May study measured a different kind of visibility. It reported 6.04 million BTC, or 30.2% of issued supply, using visibility of the public key needed for a spend as its test. The November census includes script matches and divides by BTC in unspent outputs. Measuring a change over time would require a common definition and denominator.
To turn the new census into priorities for a future migration, researchers would need to examine the matched outputs and identify where a spending path depends on a visible, usable key.
items.title: Over 7 million Bitcoin could face a quantum security reckoning after new discovery

items.author: Oluwapelumi Adejumo
items.content:
Quick Take
- Anthropic-linked futures traded around $104 on Nov. 19, about 25% above the company’s $83 IPO price.
- Token Terminal tracked a record $186 million in open interest on Hyperliquid before the listing, with nearly three traders long for every trader short.
- Block Scholes found that moves in tech stocks, gold, the dollar and Treasury yields lined up with much of Bitcoin’s decline.
Crypto futures tied to Anthropic traded about 25% above the company’s IPO price on Thursday. The bets swelled during a Bitcoin selloff, but research from Block Scholes points to a broader retreat from risk rather than clear evidence that investors sold Bitcoin to buy Anthropic.
Anthropic priced 980 million shares at $83 on Nov. 18, above its initial $70 to $78 range. The base offering totaled $81 billion, including shares sold by existing holders, and valued the company at about $1.5 trillion. It surpassed SpaceX’s June IPO. Anthropic set Nov. 19 as the expected Nasdaq debut for its shares under the symbol ANT.
Ten offerings reproduced from an App Economy Insights graphic. Gross proceeds at IPO, rounded to the nearest $1 billion in the image; not corporate valuations. Excludes over-allotment options and secondary listings. Agricultural Bank of China and ICBC include both Hong Kong and Shanghai tranches. Historical exact amounts differ slightly because of rounding and source conventions.
Across 19 venues, the median price for Anthropic-linked perpetual futures was about $104 at 14:18 UTC on Nov. 19, roughly 25% above the $83 offer price, OptimistFi reported. The contracts track a reference price and do not give holders ownership of Anthropic shares.
Bitcoin had tested support near $62,000 twice by Thursday as traders watched for signs of returning demand.
What drove Bitcoin’s selloff?
In research shared with CryptoSlate, crypto derivatives analytics firm Block Scholes found that Bitcoin’s selloff broadly tracked weakness across other markets.
The firm's research analyst, Thahbib Rahman, examined Bitcoin's relationship with the Nasdaq-100 between January and September and found that a 1% move in the technology-heavy index corresponded, on average, with a 1.03% move in BTC in the same direction.
Block Scholes estimated an 11% Bitcoin decline from the Nasdaq-100’s performance alone. Including changes in gold, the US dollar and Treasury yields raised the model’s estimate to 14%, still short of the 22% drop the firm used for comparison.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded about $3 billion in net outflows in November through Nov. 18, according to daily fund-flow data from Farside Investors.
The firm's analysis of previous stock market listings also challenges the capital-flight narrative.
Among 17 US IPOs that raised at least $900 million this year, Bitcoin declined during the preceding 50 days in nine cases, showing no consistent pattern of selling ahead of major offerings.
Crypto traders valued Anthropic at up to $1.8 trillion before its listing
While Bitcoin has struggled, cryptocurrency derivatives markets have experienced a surge in trading tied to Anthropic's valuation.
Token Terminal reported that traders had speculated on Anthropic through perpetual futures on Hyperliquid for more than a year.
These markets valued the AI company at approximately $339 billion a year ago. By Nov. 18, the implied valuation had climbed to between $1.7 trillion and $1.8 trillion, well above the $1.5 trillion valuation established by the IPO.
Cash-settled Hyperliquid perpetuals, not Anthropic shares, through Nov. 18, 2026. tradeXYZ and Paragon per-share contracts converted assuming 18B shares; Entropy and Ventuals quote valuation directly. Ventuals history between annotated $339B opening and $1.61T close approximated from the screenshot ($20B rounding). Entropy and tradeXYZ daily history comes from independent Hyperliquid data, not Token Terminal exports. Entropy Nov. 16-17 is screenshot-estimated; Nov. 18 is annotated. Paragon has only a Nov. 18 figure. IPO $1.5T is a rounded retrospective benchmark; null means unavailable.
Token Terminal data showed that open interest in Anthropic-linked perpetuals reached an all-time high of $186 million on Nov. 18, with all the previous week's net growth concentrated on trade[XYZ], which launched its Anthropic market on Oct. 26.
Daily trading volume peaked at $261 million on Nov. 10, coinciding with the announcement of Anthropic's initial IPO pricing range.
Bullish participation also accelerated. On Nov. 18, Token Terminal recorded 5,567 traders holding long positions, compared with 1,996 holding short positions, a nearly three-to-one ratio.
On OKX, Anthropic’s pre-IPO perpetual initially traded near 130 USDC when the company’s roadshow began, about 67% above the top of the proposed range. The run-up followed earlier leveraged bets on Anthropic’s IPO in September.
The contract subsequently declined toward 98 USDC as bankers raised the offering price, before recovering above 103 USDC following Wednesday's final pricing announcement.
Erald Ghoos, CEO of OKX Europe, told CryptoSlate that the divergence reflected a disagreement between traditional financial institutions and crypto traders over the company's valuation.
Ghoos said:
“For 10 days, traders and bankers disagreed about what Anthropic is worth. The bankers moved up to $83. Traders still think that's too low, by about 24%.”
The executive pointed to SpaceX's June listing, when pre-IPO derivatives traded within 4% of the company's eventual first-day closing price, while the stock's IPO price was approximately 16% below that close.
Block Scholes also reported growing activity on Hyperliquid, where Anthropic-linked perpetuals averaged approximately $75 million in daily trading volume since Nov. 5, up from $7 million in September.
However, those contracts represented only about 1% of Hyperliquid's overall trading volume and roughly 3% of the increase in non-crypto trading since September.
The benchmarks for Anthropic’s first day on Nasdaq are the $83 IPO price and the roughly $104 futures quote. The gap is what traders bet on, not what public-market investors paid.
items.title: Anthropic’s crypto futures traded 25% above its $81 billion IPO price as Bitcoin slumped 22%

items.author: Aaron Wise
items.content:
STRC, the stock that Michael Saylor’s Strategy wants to hold near $100 while paying ultra-high dividends, closed Wednesday at its lowest finish since August 20 and 3.9% below that $100 target.
It’s falling despite a war chest of expenditures by Strategy, including last week’s $228 million STRC buy-back, and depleting its STRC rescue fund by 89%.
Saylor proclaimed in May that keeping STRC near $100 per share was “the company’s number one business objective.”
As usual, shareholders of Strategy’s MSTR common stock suffered dilution to provide rescue funds for STRC preferreds, including $206 million of last week’s $228 million buy-back.
As of November 15, only $332 million remained of the $3 billion that Strategy’s board of directors authorized for STRC repurchases; 89% is gone.
Michael Saylor’s bull market never came
On October 29, Saylor declared, “We’re at the beginning of the next bitcoin bull market.” Since then, BTC has fallen 19%. Worse, MSTR is down 36%.
Strategy owns 850,849 BTC that it bought for $64.2 billion. At Wednesday evening’s price, those coins were worth about $53.3 billion for an unrealized loss of $10.9 billion.
Worse, Strategy has spent more than $1 billion in expenses operating this unrealized loss-generating colossus.
Notably, and although corporate cash does not reduce an unrealized capital loss, the company does have $4.9 billion in cash that it could — but probably won’t — use to offset roughly half of that loss.
All of these failures, for context, exist because Saylor believed BTC would somehow achieve a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) near 30%.
Instead, over the past five years, BTC has only rallied 7% in total.
MSTR has only rallied 24% over the same time period — rewarding patient investors with less than a single year’s worth of Saylor’s 30% annual target, despite faithfully waiting half a decade.
Read more: Michael Saylor’s STRC has been off parity for five months
$1 billion to operate a company generating $10+ billion unrealized losses
Saylor posted on Wednesday, “Seller exhaustion will come long before Saylor exhaustion.”
It helps that Saylor, unlike his common shareholders, receives executive perks regardless of the underperformance of MSTR, STRC, and BTC.
Saylor, unlike his shareholders, is in the business of selling stock. He wants people to buy what his company sells: MSTR.
Strategy has a scheduled investor Q&A with Saylor and CEO Phong Le on Thursday at 5pm New York time.
Protos reported on October 1 that 64% of an earlier, $2 billion STRC rescue fund was expended as of Strategy’s September 28 filing. Strategy subsequently increased its authorization by $1 billion and spent roughly $1.4 billion more, enabled mostly by MSTR dilution.

items.author: Andjela Radmilac
items.content:
Quick Take
- Anthropic priced its record $81 billion IPO at $83 per share ahead of its Nasdaq debut.
- The ECB warned that IPO booms have historically been followed by weaker stock returns and could complicate AI financing.
- Bitcoin traders are watching for broader market volatility as Anthropic begins trading and AI stock valuations face scrutiny.
Anthropic priced its $81 billion IPO at $83 a share Wednesday. The company behind Claude said it expected trading to begin on Nasdaq on Nov. 19. If the stock opens above $83, investors who got shares in the offering will have an immediate gain on paper. Anthropic won't get any extra cash from that move.
The net result is that Anthropic has effectively raised $81.3 billion from its public offering, with a further $26 billion private placement. This creates a $1.5 trillion fully diluted valuation despite growing concerns over AI infrastructure spending and financing risks.
The European Central Bank warned Wednesday that stock returns have tended to weaken after a rush of companies going public. Its concern is what happens when the rush ends: AI companies may still have data centers to finish and bills to pay, but could find it harder to raise cash if stock prices fall and lenders pull back. For Bitcoin and the broader crypto industry, the question is whether a pullback in AI shares becomes a wider selloff in risk assets, not whether the IPO itself takes money out of crypto.
Why a rush of IPOs gets the ECB's attention
US initial public offerings brought in about $44 billion in 2025. In its November financial stability review, the ECB cited a July analyst forecast of about $225 billion for all of 2026, alongside its staff's separate $212 billion estimate from early November. Both were made before Anthropic set its final price.
Rounded annual US IPO proceeds. 2025 is reported historical activity; the two 2026 bars are separate full-year forecasts, not additive amounts or completed offerings. The ECB staff estimate was prepared in early November using actual January–October proceeds, a seasonal forecast, and preliminary Anthropic inputs. The market-analyst projection dates to July. Both predate Anthropic’s final Nov. 18 pricing.
It's easier to see why offerings tend to bunch together from the company's side. If investors are willing to pay more for each share, a company can raise the same amount of cash by selling a smaller piece of itself. Other companies see those terms and have a reason to get their own deals done before demand cools.
The ECB compared the size of each quarter's IPOs relative to the economy with what the broader stock market returned over the next two years. In the US, higher issuance went with weaker returns, but the relationship accounted for only about a tenth of the variation. It tells us more about the conditions in which companies choose to sell shares than it does about where Anthropic will trade this afternoon.
Selling shares gives a company cash it doesn't have to repay. If the price drops, shareholders take the loss, and the company keeps the money it already raised. The trouble starts when a business still needs money to finish building and has fewer ways to raise it. Borrowers still owe interest, and AI companies can still owe rent for computing space they no longer need. When a data-center operator borrows against its tenants' payments, the people buying those data-center bonds are counting on the tenants to keep paying.
The ECB’s review of AI borrowing extends that risk beyond shareholders: if lenders start doubting projects will bring in enough cash, they can charge more or stop funding new ones, even as falling stock prices make raising money by selling shares more expensive. The ECB said the issuance surge and the rise of passive investing do not currently pose a systemic risk.
Where the $81 billion goes
When a company goes public, it sells newly created shares to raise money, and people who already own shares can sell some of theirs in the same deal. Anthropic will be doing both.
Its final terms cover 980 million shares at $83 each. About $79 billion goes to Anthropic for the new shares and $2 billion goes to existing shareholders, before fees in both cases. That excludes an option for the banks running the deal to buy up to 147 million additional shares. Anthropic also arranged a separate $26 billion private placement with strategic partners, contingent on the IPO closing.
Gross proceeds at the $83 offer price: $79.38 billion for Anthropic and $1.96 billion for selling stockholders, totaling $81.34 billion before underwriting discounts and other expenses. Calculated from the final share allocation. Excludes the underwriters’ option to buy 147 million additional shares; does not represent money raised through subsequent Nasdaq trading.
- Anthropic: new sharesUSD 79.38B97.6%
- Selling stockholders: existing sharesUSD 1.96B2.4%
Those banks are the underwriters. They take indications of how many shares investors want and what they're willing to pay, then help the company set the price and decide who gets shares. Under the deal's underwriting terms, the banks agree to buy the shares from Anthropic and the selling shareholders and resell them to investors. They're paid through a discount: the banks pay the sellers less per share than the investors pay. If you got an allocation, you were assigned a number of shares at $83. If you buy after trading starts, you pay the market price, and the money goes to the investor selling you the shares.
The money Anthropic gets from selling new stock gives it more room to pay for the equipment and computing capacity it needs to run Claude. Its IPO filing puts expected payments on contractual commitments at $71 billion over the 12 months after Sept. 30, including $4 billion tied to arrangements with conditions or termination rights. Those are primarily commitments for computing and infrastructure, not a loan coming due or a bill the IPO was specifically set up to pay.
The company also reported $147 billion in liquidity as of Sept. 30, before the IPO and private placement, so the commitments do not by themselves indicate an immediate cash shortfall. They give a sense of why access to funding counts long after the first trade. The stock is due to start trading Thursday, while Anthropic expects the offering itself to close Friday if the usual conditions are met.
What to watch when Anthropic starts trading
Anthropic is due to trade under the ticker ANT. Nasdaq's regular session starts at 9:30 a.m. New York time, but the stock doesn't have to open at that hour. The exchange runs an opening auction for IPOs, collecting buy and sell orders and finding the price at which the most shares can change hands. The first trade tells you how that initial batch of orders matched. The closing price will show whether buyers were still willing to pay as much after a session of trading.
Index funds can bring another set of buyers later. These funds aim to match a specified list of stocks, so when an index adds a company, the funds that follow it generally adjust their holdings. MSCI says Anthropic would enter its broad investable market indexes at the Nov. 30 close, effective Dec. 1, if it qualifies for early entry. Which funds would buy depends on the exact index each one tracks.
The ECB found that companies already on the market tended to sell more stock when index funds owned a larger share of them. Its researchers think the prospect of those buyers arriving soon after listing could help some companies raise more at their IPO, too. They didn't estimate how much of Anthropic's $83 price came from that expectation.
Crypto traders already have contracts tied to Anthropic's share price. The Nasdaq debut gives them an actual share price to compare those contracts with. Bitcoin‘s 30-day correlation with the Nasdaq-100 stood at 0.7 in Talos's Nov. 12 report, pointing to sensitivity to the same shifts in investor risk appetite. But a move in both on Thursday wouldn't establish that investors sold Bitcoin to buy ANT.
Even a strong first day would tell us only what buyers were willing to pay for Anthropic now. The ECB's warning is about whether AI companies can still raise cash on reasonable terms when investors are less eager, and the bills are still coming due.

items.author: Decrypt Staff
items.content:
In brief
- Some 21% of Gen Z adults own crypto, compared with 16% who have an employer retirement plan and 3% of baby boomers who own crypto, according to SoFi’s survey.
- Only 13% of all Americans own crypto, 62% are firm skeptics, and 77% call it a “side quest” they don’t have time or energy for.
- SoFi argues that offering crypto through banks would boost adoption, with 63% of current investors saying they’d trade more at their primary bank.
For many young Americans, crypto is coming before the 401(k).
Some 21% of Gen Z adults own cryptocurrency, compared with 16% who hold an employer-sponsored retirement plan like a 401(k), according to a survey released Thursday by SoFi Technologies.
That’s seven times the rate of baby boomers, just 3% of whom own crypto. Crypto was Gen Z’s most widely held investment in the survey, ahead of stocks, bonds ,and real estate.
The online survey of 2,064 U.S. adults was conducted by SoFi and YouGov from Oct. 15 to 28. SoFi, a nationally chartered bank that sells crypto alongside checking and investment accounts, developed the report with Culture Co-op.
Gen Z respondents described crypto less as a gamble than a strategy. They were nearly three times as likely as the general population to call it one of the best ways to build future wealth, 21% vs. 8%, and 61% said they see it as a financial advantage unique to their generation.
Only 20% of Gen Z crypto owners said they bought in because it “sounded interesting,” compared with 34% of crypto investors overall. Diversification (32%) and easier international payments (29%) ranked higher.
Part of the gap reflects age. Many respondents in their late teens and 20s don’t yet have access to an employer retirement plan.
Across the broader population, the picture is far cooler. Only 13% of Americans own crypto, and 62% are firm skeptics. Three in four say crypto feels intimidating to get into, and 77% agreed with the statement, “Cryptocurrency feels like a financial side quest that I don’t have the time or energy for.”
Even owners feel out of their depth: 82% of current crypto investors said they should know more about it than they do, and 11% admitted knowing little to nothing.
“Nobody feels the gaps in their financial education more sharply than someone who has just bought Bitcoin,” said Natalie Brunell, host of the Coin Stories podcast and a contributor to SoFi’s crypto newsletter.
The findings echo a recent survey conducted by Ipsos for the DeFi Education Fund, which found that 22% of Americans have ever owned or used crypto but only 13% used it in the past year.
SoFi argues that putting crypto in the same app as banking is the key to wider adoption. Half of respondents open to crypto said having their primary bank offer it would be a tipping point, and 63% of current investors said they’d trade more if they could do it at their bank.
SoFi has been building out that model, launching a tokenized deposit that pays 4.4% and moves like a stablecoin, as well as a bank-issued stablecoin running on Polygon’s payments infrastructure.
The survey also challenges the crypto “tech bro” stereotype. Black and Hispanic respondents own crypto at more than twice the rate of white respondents, 22% to 9%. Miami led the 10 cities surveyed at 20% ownership, while San Francisco matched the national average at 13%.

items.author: Bennett Tomlin
items.content:
Anthropic’s IPO today will be one of the largest in history, both in terms of the amount raised and in the valuation of the firm itself.
The AI giant expects to offer its shares at a price of $83, valuing it at over $1 trillion, upsized from its original filings.
Additionally, Anthropic is offering an additional placement of its Class N (non-voting) shares to certain partners that would raise an additional $26 billion.
In total, if underwriters also take advantage of their opportunity to purchase additional shares, then the prospectus predicts the Anthropic IPO will have net proceeds of “approximately $117.0 billion.”
Anthropic’s valuation at the time of IPO will be less than SpaceX’s.
Read more: Anthropic was keeping its IPO share price secret — footnote reveals $71.43
Anthropic’s founders have structured things so that they’ll maintain more than 50% of the votes in the firm, using an entity called Founder LLC.
This is despite the fact that they’ll own a much smaller portion, aided by the extra votes of their special Class F shares.
The founders also have their own Class A shares that also give them additional votes.
Anthropic’s Financials
Anthropic will be heading into this IPO with massive losses totaling over $100 billion for the year so far. These are mostly accounting-driven and related to convertible notes.
When you take Anthropic’s adjustments into account, the last two quarters have both had a positive adjusted net income.
Anthropic has also claimed that its revenue has passed what it spends on compute, though for the most recent quarter its compute bill grew approximately 77%, while its revenue grew “only” 47%.
However, in absolute terms, its revenue still grew faster than the spending on compute.
Anthropic’s partnerships do have a cost, though.
In many cases, the company has committed to spending tens of billions with these firms like Amazon, Google, and Broadcom.
Interestingly, for the year so far, Anthropic discloses that approximately 5-7% of its revenue came from customers who were eventually found to be breaking the rules, and it warned, “Customers may evade our controls, and customers whose access is restricted or terminated may re-register under new accounts.
“As a result, revenue from such customers may continue or recur notwithstanding our enforcement efforts.”
Anthropic further disclosed that its “top five customers represented approximately 25% of our revenue for the nine months ended September 30, 2026.”
It also disclosed that approximately 71% of its revenue came from the US.
Read more: Anthropic outranks most IPOs in history
Super-intelligence
One of the fascinating changes that has come about as this S-1 has been amended is related to its usage of “Super Intelligence.”
The original S-1 didn’t use the term “Super Intelligence” or “SI” to describe any part of its business. Its only use of the term being the name of the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence.
However, its most recent amended version does use the term.
Now it notes, “For purposes of this prospectus, to avoid confusion, we use the terms ‘super intelligence,’ ‘SI,’ ‘artificial intelligence,’ and ‘AI’ interchangeably.
On September 29, 2026, the US president issued Executive Order 14434, which directs federal executive departments and agencies to use the terms ‘Super Intelligence’ and ‘SI’ in place of ‘Artificial Intelligence’ and ‘AI.'”
What are the risks?
Anthropic’s S-1 for this IPO includes many risks, some of which are boilerplate, but it also notes some interesting risks.
These include:
- “Our models have in the past behaved, and may in the future behave, in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed”
- “The political environment and our engagement with policymakers and public positions on AI regulation and safety could subject us to heightened scrutiny, political backlash, or disproportionate regulatory action”
- “Our sales to government entities and highly regulated organizations are subject to challenges and risks”
- “Unfavorable media coverage regarding our business, our models, platform, and applications, the impacts of AI, and the AI industry more broadly could adversely affect our business”
- “Many of the risks we face are interconnected and may compound or trigger cascading adverse effects across our business, which could amplify their overall impact.”
SpaceX
One of the inevitable comparisons for Anthropic is SpaceX, another massive recent IPO in the AI industry.
For one thing, both firms have connections to another AI heavyweight, OpenAI.
Elon Musk, who leads SpaceX, was previously the OpenAI co-chair and would eventually merge xAI into SpaceX.
Similarly, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was previously OpenAI’s vice president of research.
Daniela Amodei, the president and chair of Anthropic, was previously OpenAI’s vice president of safety.
SpaceX and Anthropic are also linked because Anthropic buys substantial amounts of compute that Anthropic purchases from SpaceX.
Read more: DoorDash has outperformed SpaceX by 48% since IPO
More than one-third of SpaceX revenue for quarter three came from this “Customer B,” its unnamed customer who’s spending lines up with Anthropic.
The two firms are also similar in other ways, even raising similar amounts in their IPO.
In both cases, the founders have kept voting control of their firms.
Both even had similar revenue in quarter three of this year.
FTX
People have inevitably brought up Sam Bankman-Fried’s theft from his customers when they talk about Anthropic.
One of the dozens of investments he made with stolen funds was in Anthropic. The initial increase in value of this firm was one of the things that made it possible for customers to receive back the amount they had in dollar amounts on the day of bankruptcy despite the billions in misappropriated funds.
Caroline Ellison and Nishad Singh also had equity in Anthropic but forfeited it after they pleaded guilty.
Read more: Manifund hires Caroline Ellison while fighting FTX over $1.5M
Those shares would, of course, be worth even more now than then, but that doesn’t change the fundamental nature of the crime.
