items.author: Cointelegraph by Isabelle Castro
items.content:
Tether invokes The Big Short in swipe at S&P over USDT reserve risks
S&P Global made no downward adjustment in its latest Stablecoin Stability Assessment, as 5 is the lowest available score.
S&P Global Ratings has kept Tether’s USDt at the lowest level on its stablecoin stability scale as riskier assets take up a growing share of the token’s reserves.
In a report published Nov. 18, S&P scored USDt’s ability to hold its dollar peg at 5 (weak). The assessment is unchanged from November 2025.
Higher-risk holdings, including gold, Bitcoin (BTC), public equities, secured loans and corporate bonds, were equivalent to 28% of USDt (USDT) in circulation as of Sept. 30, up from 24% a year earlier. “A significant drop in the value of these assets could lead to USDT being undercollateralized,” S&P said in the report.
“The problem is S&P’s framework, not our reserves,” Tether told Cointelegraph. “Their own history shows the underlying problem,” it added, referencing The Big Short, the film about the 2008 financial crisis.
Tether’s Sept. 30 reserve report, attested by BDO, showed approximately $191.5 billion in assets against $183.5 billion in liabilities, leaving roughly $7.95 billion in excess assets. The agency added that it found further weaknesses but made no downward adjustment “because our assessment cannot be lower than 5.”
S&P questions reserve oversight safeguards
Among the additional weaknesses highlighted by S&P was the regulatory oversight of El Salvador, where Tether relocated in January 2025.
According to the report, the National Commission of Digital Assets of El Salvador (CNAD), the regulatory body which oversees Tether in the country, requires 70% of the reserves to be held in assets that can be liquidated within 30 days. The company said they considered the framework “broad,” allowing for the inclusion of relatively high-risk assets like gold, BTC and loans.
The S&P also pointed to the lack of a requirement to segregate the reserve assets, unlike those expected by regulators in the US and Europe. As there is no publicly available information about segregation, the report states, there is no insight into how they are insulated from broader corporate risks.
USDT’s breakdown of reserve assets. Source S&P Global
Audit disclosure remains a concern
In August 2026, KPMG confirmed they had issued an unqualified opinion on Tether’s 2025 accounts, in the company’s first “full independent audit”. The issuer highlighted that the audit supported the financial statements issued by the company.
However, S&P said the audited statements and the auditor’s report have not been published, which limits its ability to check the underlying information. Reserve reports also do not name the custodians and counterparties holding Tether’s assets, S&P said, and attestations remain quarterly while other stablecoins generally report monthly.
Related: Tether backs Bolivian fintech bringing USDT payments to food delivery and banking
At the time of S&P’s initial downgrade in 2025, Tether disputed the result. CEO Paolo Ardoino wrote on X, “we wear your loathing with pride,” pointing to past financial collapses as “proof” that traditional systems are broken.
Although the stability rating remained at 5, S&P ended the Nov. 18 report noting that Tether had maintained a good history of price stability, particularly in the last 12 months.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- All four chatbots provided information for potentially deadly attacks in under 12 hours, a congressional watchdog found.
- Investigators verified the feasibility of the plans but did not carry out attacks, and the tests cannot rank the models' safety.
- Senator Maggie Hassan wants hearings on AI safety as technology companies contend with a surge of software vulnerabilities and patches.
Four of the most widely used AI chatbots helped government investigators develop potentially deadly attack plans in less than 12 hours, despite safeguards intended to stop exactly that kind of request.
OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, Google's Gemini and Grok all supplied usable information during covert testing by the Government Accountability Office, according to a report released Wednesday. Investigators posed as attackers, then checked the responses against real locations, available materials, and expert assessments.
Two systems assisted with plans involving improvised explosives in crowded U.S. cities. Two others supplied information for attacks on electrical infrastructure, according to the watchdog, which withheld the models' assignments and operational details to prevent copycat attempts.
Senator Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the investigation, warned that a terrorist could obtain "a concrete playbook for how to carry out a deadly attack" in less than 12 hours, according to her statement.
Safeguards that didn't hold
The chatbots initially activated protections, including refusing requests, removing harmful information or suspending accounts. Investigators bypassed those barriers with common jailbreak techniques, which manipulate an AI system into ignoring its safety rules.
The GAO checked suggested locations, researched whether materials were available and consulted specialists about the plans' feasibility. Some answers contained errors, including misplaced roads on a map, and investigators did not construct explosives or execute an attack.
In the report, "viable" means somebody would likely be able to follow the information supplied, not that an attack was demonstrated to succeed. Each model was tested on one assigned scenario, and the agency said the results were not statistically representative or suitable for ranking the companies.
OpenAI and Google said the tests involved older models, while Anthropic acknowledged that determined users can sometimes extract harmful material. The companies described continuing improvements to safety systems, though the GAO concluded those protections failed in its tests.
This is not really new. The findings follow a previous research showing eight of 10 popular chatbots assisted simulated teenage users planning violent attacks. The separate study tested 720 responses and found the bots provided actionable help roughly three-quarters of the time.
AI's other security problem
The GAO findings arrive amid outages affecting banks, Microsoft services and the National Security Agency. Officials say the disruptions were separate incidents, not evidence of a coordinated AI-driven cyberattack, even as the rush to repair software flaws has created its own problems.
Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton connected the NSA's outage to patching work. Officials described the recent breakdowns as maintenance-related, although individual organizations offered different explanations for their failures.
AI tools now find vulnerabilities faster than human teams can test and deploy fixes. Last month, the AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP flaws pushed website operators into an urgent patching campaign; the software powers a large share of the web.
The sheer volume is becoming another problem. VulnCheck data reveals there have been more than 100,000 software vulnerabilities logged this year by November 13, more than twice the total for 2025. Engineers still have to evaluate and deploy fixes without breaking the systems they are meant to protect.
That acceleration cuts both ways. Defenders gain powerful tools for finding weaknesses, but hasty repairs can disrupt essential systems, and malicious users may gain faster access to attack planning.
Hassan said she will make AI safety legislation an early priority when she takes over the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in January. She plans hearings examining risks to public safety and critical infrastructure; the GAO itself made no formal policy recommendations.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Palmer Luckey revealed SLAB, a proposed ocean platform designed to last 1,000 years and allow American industries to operate outside certain state and local regulations.
- Luckey says the project received funding at a $1 billion valuation in 2017, but has not disclosed its location, construction status or operating timeline.
- In an exchange on X, Luckey said he wants people to access medicine currently illegal in the United States, raising questions about the limits of offshore regulation.
Palmer Luckey, the billionaire founder of Oculus and defense technology company Anduril, is spending over a billion dollars to have a private island where he can do things without worrying about U.S. laws.
He wants to build a massive industrial platform in the ocean where American businesses can operate without some of the regulations they face on land. And he has apparently been working on the idea for nearly a decade.
In an X post published Wednesday, Luckey revealed a project called SLAB, a proposed seastead with a 1,000-year design life that he says could support industries ranging from metal processing and oil refining to medical research and treatment.
Selling Oculus to Facebook in 2014 gave me money for helicopter flight lessons and developing a seastead called SLAB with a 1,000 year design life.
The goal was to be cheaper than land and absent state/local laws that cripple critical American industries like metal processing,… pic.twitter.com/aJkd0eOgLF
— Palmer Luckey (@PalmerLuckey) November 18, 2026
His goal, he wrote, is to create an industrial base cheaper than land and free from state and local laws that he believes are crippling critical American industries. Luckey described the project as a way to strengthen the United States rather than escape it, calling it a "relief valve" for outdated regulations.
“Me and a few close friends cashed it up at a $1B valuation back in 2017, and while it still has a long way to go, there has been significant progress towards my goal of reviving manifest destiny and westward expansion,” he wrote.
Luckey said he used proceeds from Facebook's 2014 acquisition of Oculus to finance the project.
The announcement included an AI-generated illustration of a gigantic offshore platform, rather than photographs of an operating facility so it’s hard to know which type of endeavor he’s dedicating his time and money to.
Luckey said he decided to disclose SLAB after learning that journalists were preparing to describe it as a floating AI data center. He rejected that characterization as incomplete, saying the project was considerably older and "way cooler than that."
Medical treatments outside US regulations
Luckey provided a more specific indication of his ambitions in a heated exchange with journalist Joshua Topolsky, who questioned whether creating an offshore community was a sensible way to modernize medical research.
Topolsky argued that regulatory reform could happen without constructing an island in the ocean and challenged Luckey to identify which existing rules had prevented him from pursuing medical advances.
Luckey responded that he would rather build a place where people could save their families with "safe but currently illegal medicine ASAP" than wait for lawmakers to reform the system.
He accused political interests and large pharmaceutical companies of obstructing change, arguing that conventional reform would require legislation capable of securing support from 60 senators.
Does moving offshore actually escape American law?
Luckey's plan also faces a significant legal complication: moving an operation into the ocean does not automatically place it outside American jurisdiction.
When another X user asked how close SLAB could operate to San Francisco without falling under its jurisdiction, Luckey answered, "Three miles."
That generally corresponds to the boundary of California's state-controlled coastal waters, according to the U.S. Bureau of Ocean Energy Management.
That said, federal jurisdiction extends considerably farther. The United States has a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea and a 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zone, where it retains authority over certain economic activities and the construction and use of artificial islands, according to NOAA guidance.
The applicable rules would depend on SLAB's location, whether it floats or is attached to the seabed, and how it is registered. Even vessels operating on the high seas remain subject to applicable maritime laws and the jurisdiction of their flag states, so it’s not as if he’d be living in an anarchist fairy tale.
Medical research presents its own complications, if that’s what he’s actually doing. The FDA requires foreign clinical studies submitted in support of U.S. drug approvals to meet good clinical practice standards, including independent ethical review and informed consent. Conducting treatment offshore would not, by itself, make an unapproved drug legal for sale in the United States.
Previous seasteading experiments have encountered similar jurisdictional disputes. A floating community off Thailand triggered a confrontation with authorities in 2019, while a subsequent project in Panama adopted boat registration to operate within an existing legal framework.
This is all, of course, speculation. Luckey has not publicly identified SLAB's proposed location, the specific regulations it would avoid, or the medical treatments he hopes to make available. He has also not announced a construction deadline or provided independently verifiable details of the project's current physical development.

Ledger warns Berlin customers as hardware wallet tampering investigation expands
Ledger advised customers who purchased devices in Berlin since January 2026 to contact support as it investigates suspected hardware implants in Germany and Dubai.
Ledger has warned customers who purchased hardware wallets in Berlin since January 2026 to contact its support team as the company investigates reports of tampered devices in Germany and the United Arab Emirates.
In a Wednesday update, Ledger said its investigation into a hardware wallet tampering campaign had identified several suspicious devices in Berlin. The company also acknowledged reports of tampered devices in Dubai, where two customers recently reported losing a combined $604,000 in cryptocurrency.
Ledger said the incidents were connected to the same distribution-channel tampering campaign first investigated in Southeast Asia in October, when the company asked authorized reseller CryptoBilis to suspend sales and shipments amid reports of cryptocurrency thefts. Ledger also confirmed that one Ledger Nano Gen 5 had been affected in the region.
According to the hardware wallet maker, all confirmed tampered devices contained similar physical modifications designed to capture users’ recovery phrases during setup. The company said it had found no vulnerability in its secure chip or operating system and no confirmed cases involving devices purchased directly from its website.
Ledger is also offering physical inspections, including X-ray analysis, at its factory in Vierzon, France, for customers concerned their devices may have been compromised.

items.author: Oluwapelumi Adejumo
items.content:
Quick Take
- Germany's Bundestag approved a bill allowing customs to freeze suspicious Bitcoin holdings, including assets stored in self-custody wallets.
- Authorities could restrict crypto transfers for up to 180 days without controlling private keys, challenging the legal freedom of self-custody holders.
- Identifying wallet owners and enforcing transfer bans remain major hurdles, while the legislation awaits final approval.
Germany's parliament has approved legislation allowing customs authorities to freeze suspicious crypto holdings, including assets stored in self-custody wallets.
The Bundestag passed the bill on Nov. 12, advancing a broader government effort to combat money laundering and financial crime by expanding authorities' powers to investigate assets of questionable origin.
Under the proposed legislation, German customs could temporarily freeze significant assets, including cryptocurrencies, when factual evidence raises doubts about their lawful origin.
The approved committee text identifies assets worth more than €100,000 as a general benchmark for significant holdings. Authorities could also combine closely connected assets when determining whether they qualify.
Customs would initially have 30 days to investigate suspicious holdings, with a finance court authorized to extend the restriction by another 150 days if investigators demonstrate credible doubts about their origin and grounds for further investigation.
The legislation, however, has not completed its final approval process. As of Nov. 18, final consideration by the Bundesrat, Germany's chamber representing the states, and publication in the Federal Law Gazette remained outstanding.
Germany's Bitcoin freeze powers face a self-custody challenge
The proposed rules could have different consequences depending on whether investors hold their Bitcoin through centralized exchanges or control their wallets directly.
For assets held on an exchange, German authorities could issue an enforceable attachment order requiring the custodian to restrict withdrawals from an affected account.
The mechanism draws on Germany's existing tax enforcement provisions, which allow authorities to prevent third parties from releasing assets subject to a legally enforceable attachment.
However, enforcing similar restrictions against self-custody wallets presents a more complicated challenge.
Unlike centralized exchanges, self-custody wallets allow users to control the private keys needed to authorize Bitcoin transactions without relying on a financial intermediary.
Germany's proposed framework addresses such holdings by treating cryptocurrencies as attachable property rights.
Under Section 321 of the German Fiscal Code, authorities can attach certain property rights without involving a third party by serving the holder with a legal prohibition on disposing of them.
Applied to eligible self-custodied Bitcoin, this could prohibit an owner from transferring the affected assets without automatically removing their ability to authorize blockchain transactions.
Consequently, an individual could remain technically capable of moving Bitcoin despite being legally prohibited from doing so.
Germany's Blockchain Bundesverband highlighted this enforcement challenge in a submission on an earlier version of the legislation. The industry association explained that authorities must distinguish between cryptocurrencies held by custodians and assets controlled directly by individuals.
It also warned that identifying a blockchain wallet does not necessarily establish who controls its assets, particularly where multiple parties share transaction-signing authority.
These complications could make enforcing restrictions on self-custody wallets harder than freezing balances held by regulated exchanges.
The legislation also distinguishes temporary asset freezes from permanent confiscation, which would require a separate finance court decision establishing that the property originated unlawfully.
Should the bill complete Germany's legislative process, its effectiveness against self-custodied crypto holdings will depend on authorities' ability to identify wallet controllers and enforce legal restrictions without direct control of their private keys.
items.title: Germany moves to freeze Bitcoin for up to 180 days, even without access to private keys

items.content:
Bain Capital Crypto leads $110M Variational round at $1.5B valuation
Variational raised $110 million at a $1.5 billion valuation to expand Omni’s derivatives markets and increase trading limits.
Onchain derivatives trading platform Variational has raised $110 million in a funding round led by Bain Capital Crypto, valuing the company at $1.5 billion as it seeks to challenge traditional brokerages by connecting crypto traders with liquidity from established financial markets.
The Series B round also received backing from Dragonfly, HSG, Peak XV and 50T Funds, according to the company’s Wednesday announcement.
Variational powers Omni, a platform offering leveraged exposure to more than 550 crypto and traditional markets. Unlike Hyperliquid, which maintains separate order books for its markets, Variational aggregates liquidity from onchain and off-chain sources, including Hyperliquid itself, a company spokesperson told Cointelegraph.
“Our unique model allows us to bridge off-chain liquidity to on-chain traders,” the spokesperson said, adding that liquidity from its unnamed tier-one market maker remains off-chain.
Since launching in early 2025, Omni has processed more than $475 billion in trading volume across over 100,000 accounts, the company said. Traditional markets now account for more than half of its daily trading volume.
Variational also launched its swaps product in September, which has since generated more than $80 billion in trading volume, according to the company.
Variational looks to compete with traditional brokerages
Despite traditional assets accounting for most daily trading volume, Variational’s customers remain primarily crypto-native retail traders, a company spokesperson told Cointelegraph. Asked about competing with traditional brokerages such as Robinhood and Interactive Brokers, the spokesperson pointed to the need to make the platform more accessible to users unfamiliar with cryptocurrency.
Related: Hyperliquid Strategies seeks futures registration for perps
“The platform needs to abstract away the ‘crypto’ feel,” the spokesperson said, adding that the company is developing email-based account registration and alternative deposit methods to remove the current requirements for crypto wallets and USDC.
Variational faces stiff competition in onchain derivatives trading. Hyperliquid recorded approximately $274 billion in reported trading volume over the past 30 days, compared with $82 billion for Lighter and $62 billion for Variational, according to DeFiLlama data at the time of writing on Wednesday. Variational also ranked third in open interest at approximately $688 million, behind Hyperliquid’s $5.7 billion and Aster’s $1.2 billion.

items.author: Cointelegraph by Bryan O'Shea
items.content:
Binance says it obtained $6.5B worldwide freezing order after hack
The court orders allow legal notices to be served via blockchain and provide for a continuously updated list of 26,000 wallet addresses linked to stolen assets, Binance’s lawyers said.
Binance said it has secured a $6.5 billion worldwide freezing injunction from the Abu Dhabi Global Market Courts as it seeks to recover assets stolen in its record Oct. 29 hack.
The court orders target unidentified perpetrators of the attack and are intended to help issuers, exchanges and other partners freeze and return stolen assets, the company said in a statement shared with Cointelegraph on Wednesday.
The orders can be served via blockchain, according to M. Kendall Day of Gibson Dunn, which represents Binance. This allows legal notices to be delivered to wallet addresses rather than through traditional channels. Day said market participants would also be notified of updates to a “living list” of 26,000 wallet addresses identified as holding stolen assets.
Binance said some businesses require formal court orders before they can release, transfer or return frozen funds. The injunction’s $6.5 billion amount is not a tally of recovered assets, and the statement did not disclose how much had so far been returned under the orders.
Binance also said it obtained orders requiring stolen assets to be handed over. Separate interim orders cover assets frozen by certain named parties against whom no wrongdoing is alleged.
Binance pursues stolen asset recovery
The legal action follows other efforts to secure the stolen funds in the wake of the hack, the largest-ever in the crypto industry. As Cointelegraph reported on Nov. 13, the US Justice Department said it had obtained court authorization to seize or restrain more than $1.2 billion in assets stolen from Binance. That amount was part of more than $2.7 billion frozen through government and private sector efforts, the DOJ said.
Related: Binance hack may push institutions to outside custody, FalconX exec says
As Cointelegraph previously reported, the attackers converted stolen stablecoins into assets such as Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH), which cannot be frozen, as they lack a central issuer. Blocking the stolen tokens also does not mean they’ll be returned to Binance.
Binance said last week it had since completed coverage of affected assets after committing more than $6.34 billion from its various treasury, Secure Asset Fund for Users and insurance funds. Still, replenishing customer assets is separate from recovering the stolen cryptocurrencies from the hack.
Related: North Korea denies role in $6.3B Binance hack, points finger at US
Binance pursues expansion across Asia
Separately, Binance’s Asia-Pacific head SB Seker told Reuters on Wednesday that the exchange plans to enter five Asian markets in 2027, prioritizing South and Southeast Asia. He did not name the markets and said details were expected in the first quarter.
Seker also said Binance did not need fresh capital to absorb the losses from the October hack.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Google is rolling out Genie 4 to eligible AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie, after announcing the model in October.
- Users can change generated worlds during exploration, with AI-created ambient audio and interactive character dialogue.
- Project Genie also adds an AI creation assistant, a community gallery, and longer sessions for the older Genie 3 model.
Google is opening Genie 4 to eligible AI Ultra subscribers, letting people create digital worlds they can walk through, change with a text prompt, and even populate with characters that talk back.
The company announced Wednesday that its latest world model is rolling out through Project Genie, a browser-based experiment for generating interactive environments. Genie 4 was unveiled in October, but access until now had been limited to trusted testers.
Instead of rendering a finished video from a prompt, Genie generates the scene as someone explores it. With the fourth model, users can type instructions midway through a session to change the weather, introduce a character, or steer what's happening without starting over.
#1 Searched Person on Google 2026?
Genie 4 also creates sound alongside the visuals, from wind and footsteps to dialogue that reacts to events in the scene. Google says the model improves the way people move and objects respond to physical forces, though those claims come from its own demonstrations rather than independent testing.
Now, the not so nice thing you need to know. The update is part of the Google AI Ultra subscription, which costs $199.99 per month in the United States. Google says eligible Ultra users can access the new experience now, while AI Pro subscribers can join a waitlist.
A genie that keeps getting better
Genie has come a long way from the side-scrolling experiments Google showed in 2024. The first version learned from more than 200,000 hours of gameplay footage and could turn a single image into a simple playable 2D environment, as Decrypt reported at the time.
Genie 2 moved the research into three-dimensional spaces later that year, allowing people or AI agents to navigate generated environments with keyboard and mouse controls. Genie 3 took another step toward continuous, real-time exploration, and Project Genie opened in January to adult Ultra subscribers in the United States.
Those early sessions lasted just 60 seconds, and character controls or physical behavior could be unreliable. Google is now keeping Genie 3 available alongside the new model, with sessions extended to three minutes, support for 360-degree panorama images, and the ability to connect multiple generated worlds into longer journeys.
That three-minute limit applies to the updated Genie 3 experience; Google did not specify a comparable session length for Genie 4 in Wednesday's announcement. Users can choose between the models depending on whether they want Genie 4's stronger visuals and audio or Genie 3's longer explorations.
The technology is not the same as a traditional game engine that builds a stable level with fully defined rules. Genie predicts what a world should look and sound like as it changes.
Google acknowledges that objects can drift or change between views, complex physics remain difficult, and generated speech or text may be inaccurate. It says Project Genie's audio and video carry SynthID watermarks and that inputs and outputs undergo safety screening.
Google has not announced when Genie 4 will become available to AI Pro subscribers beyond the new waitlist.

items.author: Aaron Wise
items.content:
Nvidia’s interim CEO has cautioned that the recently reported biggest top line in the company’s history — a record $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue — shouldn’t be considered as “filed” with the SEC.
The company has also admitted that its unpaid invoices have more than doubled from January to $81 billion.
Fueling suspicions about the quality of that $115.8 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported an SEC probe of Nvidia’s shareholder disclosures.
Short-seller Michael Burry also posted a list of doubts about Nvidia’s financials, while another famous short-seller, Carson Block, opened a new short-sale.
Nvidia furnished, not filed, its quarterly earnings
Merely “furnishing” this press release without certifying its contents, Nvidia disclaims associated liability for violations of SEC Sections 11, 12(a)(2), and 18.
Moreover, Nvidia’s extraordinary accounts receivable figure requires equally extraordinary faith that Nvidia’s customers will actually pay what they owe — especially with its stock trading at 20 times earnings.
The company “furnished” earnings numbers but declined to actually file a Form 10-Q yesterday, even though Nvidia has filed a formal 10-Q within a day of earnings for each of its last nine quarterly earnings reports without fail.
As opposed to “filed” earnings, “furnished” earnings carry no liability under Section 18 of the Securities Exchange Act, so shareholders cannot invoke it to sue over false statements, as they could over a filed report.
Sarbanes-Oxley officer certifications attach to 10-Q forms, not furnished exhibits. Those signatures attest that the financials are fairly presented.
For now, the record quarter exists only as furnished exhibits, not a certified report. Specifically, the AI chipmaker furnished Q3 results yesterday afternoon via an attachment to Form 8-K, a non-certified form.
As of publication time, Nvidia still hasn’t filed the Form 10-Q that normally would have arrived yesterday. Interim CEO Colette Kress wrote, “We plan to file our 10-Q in the coming weeks,” giving no particular reason for the delay.
Read more: YouTube beat Wall Street to the Nvidia scandal
Nvidia investors noticed
Shares momentarily rallied more than 5% after the bell, but they were trading 2% lower than yesterday’s close by 1pm. Some analysts lowered price targets, with UBS cutting its price target by $20/share, Summit Insights cutting from Buy to Hold, and other bearish actions.
Since at least 2025, every other “Magnificent Seven” stock has filed its 10-Q within one day of furnishing earnings.
Although Nvidia’s supplemental data shows China revenue, including Hong Kong, up 272% from $2.97 billion a year ago to $11 billion this quarter, the document itself cautions that Q4 forecasts assume $0 China data center compute revenue.
As an additional concern, the otherwise highly detailed press release conspicuously fails to name Jensen Huang, the company’s CEO who resigned days earlier.
Instead of being upfront, Nvidia merely mentioned “leadership transition and the search for a new chief executive officer,” as well as the board committee’s vague investigation that commenced with an incredible assertion that “the board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised” as a result of Huang’s conduct.

items.author: Decrypt Staff
items.content:
In brief
- CoinShares sold its entire corporate treasury position in Ethereum and half its Solana, freeing up $19.3 million.
- CEO Jean-Marie Mognetti framed it as capital discipline, not a bearish bet; these were small treasury positions, not client assets, and CoinShares still manages billions in both tokens.
- The sale landed amid a sharp market downturn, but the firm posted a strong quarter and is set to join the Russell indices in December.
CoinShares, one of Europe’s largest digital-asset managers, has sold its entire corporate treasury holding of Ethereum and half of its Solana.
It’s a move that might look like a loss of conviction but is really about something more prosaic: funding a stock buyback.
The decision, disclosed Tuesday in the firm’s third-quarter results, freed up $19.3 million, comprising $16.6 million from the Ethereum sale and $2.7 million from offloading half its Solana.
ETH price on November 22, 4:59PM UTC
That covers nearly half of the $40 million share-repurchase program the Jersey-based firm’s board approved in October, and the company was explicit that the proceeds are being “reallocating that capital towards share repurchases.”
CEO Jean-Marie Mognetti framed it as capital discipline rather than a bearish call. “We took the same approach to preparing for the share repurchase program,” he said, noting the sales give the company “the flexibility to act when conditions allow.”
In other words, CoinShares is converting idle treasury crypto into dry powder to buy back its own stock, which it can do under an authorization allowing repurchases of up to 25% of shares outstanding over five years.
The timing is notable. The sale lands during a brutal stretch for crypto markets. Bitcoin was trading around $63,200 on Wednesday, down from six-figure levels earlier in the cycle, while Ethereum sat near $1,770 and Solana around $74, both well off their recent highs.
Spot Ethereum ETFs, meanwhile, have bled cash for days, shedding $29.1 million on Nov. 17 to extend a multi-day outflow streak that has turned Decrypt’s ETF sentiment gauge “bearish.”
Those are precisely the risk-off conditions that have battered Bitcoin treasury firms and pressured the broader sector. For a company whose stock is poised to join the Russell indices in December, deploying capital into buybacks at depressed prices is a conventional play, even if the optics of a crypto manager selling crypto invite a second look.
In terms of scale, these were small corporate treasury positions, not client assets. CoinShares’ total assets under management recovered to $7.4 billion by quarter-end, up from $5.5 billion three months earlier, and its core business of digital-asset investment products is untouched by the treasury move.
The firm actually swung to a strong quarter, posting $39.6 million in net income as net inflows accelerated to $125 million and its lending and trading desks rebounded.
So the sale isn’t CoinShares souring on Ethereum or Solana, assets it still manages billions in on behalf of clients. It’s a treasury-management decision by a newly profitable, soon-to-be-index-listed company choosing to return capital to shareholders rather than let a modest crypto position sit on its balance sheet.

items.content:
Quick Take
- Backpack secured CFTC approval for a US futures exchange and clearinghouse, with plans to unite its global crypto derivatives business.
- The move could challenge offshore exchanges' dominance by giving American traders access to deeper international liquidity and better execution.
- Backpack has yet to disclose its launch date, initial contracts or which overseas traders can access its unified marketplace.
Crypto exchange Backpack has secured US regulatory approval to launch a futures exchange aimed at uniting American and international trading liquidity.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) designated Backpack's TLD Markets as a regulated futures exchange on Nov. 16, three days after approving its affiliated clearinghouse, TLD Clearing.
The approvals establish the regulatory foundation for Backpack to offer leveraged crypto perpetual futures to American traders while connecting them to the company's international trading operations.
However, Backpack's ambitions extend beyond entering the American derivatives market. The company wants to consolidate its global trading business under a single US-regulated exchange, eliminating the separation between domestic and overseas customers.
Backpack CEO Armani Ferrante said:
“There will be no Backpack international vs Backpack USA. Our entire platform will be operating on our CFTC regulated venue.”
The move represents a significant shift for a company that began in Chicago nearly four years ago before expanding its operations overseas.
Ferrante recalled that Backpack was “forced offshore” early in its development, prompting the company to establish operations across international markets while pursuing regulatory approval.
He described the CFTC approval as the culmination of nearly four years of work to return to the United States.
Backpack targets global crypto liquidity under US regulation
The proposed structure could reshape how American traders access cryptocurrency derivatives, particularly perpetual futures, which allow investors to maintain leveraged positions without a fixed expiration date.
Historically, regulatory restrictions have separated American crypto derivatives markets from much of the trading activity concentrated on offshore exchanges.
This fragmentation can limit available liquidity, widen the difference between buying and selling prices, and increase the cost of executing large transactions.
Backpack wants to address this by bringing eligible American and international traders into a shared order book, allowing their buy and sell orders to interact within the same regulated marketplace.
Under such an arrangement, an American trader seeking to purchase Bitcoin perpetual futures could potentially execute against sell orders submitted by overseas participants.
A larger pool of competing orders could improve market depth, narrow spreads and reduce the price impact of substantial trades.
Backpack US President Mark Wetjen said the initiative could help shift “price discovery from offshore unregulated venues to the United States.”
The company also plans to offer round-the-clock trading, support fiat and cryptocurrency collateral, and introduce cross-margining, allowing eligible positions to share available collateral.
The exchange will operate through TLD Markets, while its US-registered clearinghouse, TLD Clearing, will handle qualifying transactions.
Backpack's international reach provides an existing business to support this ambition. The company says it serves customers across more than 150 countries and regions and has processed over $450 billion in trading volume.
However, the extent to which that activity will move onto the US-regulated platform remains unclear.
Backpack has not disclosed its initial perpetual futures contracts, which overseas participants will be eligible to access the unified order book, or when trading will begin. Its US website is also currently accepting waitlist registrations.
items.title: Backpack’s US approval could threaten offshore exchanges’ grip on crypto futures trading

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Bitcoin traded near $63,060 Wednesday, down 2.8% on the day, as Anthropic prepared to price its IPO.
- Analysts disagree on whether the listing is diverting money from crypto; ETF withdrawals and liquidations offer more direct evidence.
- Bitcoin’s daily chart points to $62,000 as key support, with momentum deeply oversold.
Bitcoin fell toward $63,000 Wednesday, extending a six-week retreat just as AI developer Anthropic prepared to price one of Wall Street’s biggest initial public offerings.
The timing has revived an attractive theory: investors are selling crypto to buy AI shares.
BTC price on November 22, 4:59PM UTC
Right now Bitcoin is about to touch $62,000, down 3.8% on today’s session. Anthropic expects to price shares Wednesday at an indicated $70 to $78, ahead of Thursday’s Nasdaq debut under ANT, potentially valuing the company at $1.4 trillion, according to its IPO prospectus.
Is Anthropic draining Bitcoin?
Kraken chief economist Thomas Perfumo told MarketWatch the IPO “could also be drawing capital out of risk assets” as investors position for the sale.
That’s a theory Binance founder Changpeng Zhao shared, flagging the listing as one possible factor in Bitcoin’s decline in an X post Sunday.
Why are crypto prices down?
No one knows for sure. Correlation does not prove causation. Here are some potential reasons.
Money shifting to the Anthropic IPO: https://t.co/jYwVi4huAY
ETF outflows: U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs saw about $1.9 billion in outflows over seven trading… pic.twitter.com/XL2aB1ZL9W
— CZ 🔶 BNB (@cz_binance) November 15, 2026
There is a tempting precedent. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX listed in June and 23% in the equivalent period before Anthropic. But the comparison misses an important difference: AI stocks rallied before SpaceX; this time they have been falling alongside crypto.
“This time, the sell-off has been led by the AI trade itself,” Block Scholes research analyst Thahbib Rahman wrote in comments shared with Decrypt. Over the prior 50 days, Nvidia fell 32% and the Nasdaq dropped 11%, unlike their gains ahead of SpaceX’s IPO.
Bitcoin’s 30-day correlation with Nvidia rose from 0.20 to 0.56, while its correlation with gold fell from 0.63 to 0.39. “Liquidity is ebbing and flowing out of crypto and equities together once more,” Rahman wrote.
Bitcoin’s chart and the macro pressure
Bitcoin’s daily chart looks weak without any IPO theory. The relative strength index reads 21.8, well below the 30 threshold commonly associated with oversold markets, while an average directional index of 38.7 indicates a strong trend—in this case, downward.
The 50-day exponential moving average is also below its 200-day counterpart, a bearish configuration associated with the so-called death cross. The pattern historically signals deteriorating momentum and the possibility of further losses, although it is a lagging indicator and does not necessarily predict where prices will go next.
Also, oversold does not necessarily mean the selling has ended.
The immediate floor is around $62,000, close to Sunday’s low. Glassnode data show buyers absorbed 66,000 BTC between $62,000 and $66,000 during heavy selling, but stablecoin supply has shrunk 4.2% over 90 days. Below $62,000, the next psychological level is $60,000; resistance sits near $65,500, $69,300 and $73,700.
More tangible selling pressure has already been recorded. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $239.9 million Tuesday, including $209.5 million from BlackRock’s IBIT. Nearly $2 billion in leveraged crypto bets were liquidated during the weekend rout, amplifying losses as exchanges forcibly closed positions.
Hilbert Group portfolio manager Jesse Marre called the selloff “simply a stop loss run,” arguing that derivatives traders had already capitulated. Rising Treasury yields, a stronger dollar, and renewed expectations of Federal Reserve rate hikes also make speculative assets less attractive.
In other words, the dip is more natural market moves than money switching markets.
AI stocks are hardly celebrating
Nvidia forecast $130 billion in fourth-quarter sales, beating expectations after Jensen Huang’s abrupt departure. Yet markets remained split: global shares slipped 0.1%, while the Nasdaq gained 0.35% early and CoreWeave dropped 5.4%.
BitMEX co-founder Arthur Hayes sees the IPO less as a drain than a barometer. “Bitcoin’s going to go up too” if Anthropic soars, he said, while a weak debut could deepen pressure across risk assets.
Anthropic is scheduled to price Wednesday and start trading Thursday. Before that debut, Bitcoin must hold the same $62,000 area buyers defended during Sunday’s liquidation wave.

items.author: Jacob Lyon
items.content:
Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of GTA 6 developer Rockstar Games, has seen its shares jump by over 7% since markets opened amid gushing reviews hailing the game as a masterpiece.
GTA 6 officially released five hours ago in New Zealand, and will release internationally tomorrow.
Reviewers, however, have already had their hands on the game, and their verdicts so far have turned it into the best-reviewed game of all time on Metacritic with a near-perfect score of 99.
Washington Post game critic Gene Park described GTA 6 as “the most extraordinary game I’ve ever reviewed.”
Read more: GTA 6 leaker threatens dead man’s switch for endgame spoilers
Park, who clocked 170 hours of gameplay, described its NPC mechanics as “revolutionary” and claimed “it’s the first game since the early 3D days to make me wonder about the possibilities.”
Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier called it a “masterpiece,” and lauded it as “one of the greatest games I have ever played.”
Review success translates to share boost
Rockstar Games’ success has sent Take-Two’s share price up by 7% since yesterday’s close. Today, when the market opened at 9:30 Eastern Time, its share increased 5.6% within minutes.
Take-Two recently posted its revenue for the second quarter as $1.5 billion, falling from $1.77 billion the previous year and missing its expected $1.62 billion in revenue.
Despite this, Take-Two’s CEO Strauss Zelnick said he expects “unprecedented” GTA 6 pre-orders to “deliver an historic year for our company.”
Indeed, estimates published by Sensor Tower predict GTA 6 has sold over 17 million units and generated roughly $1.65 billion — and that’s before the game is fully released.
GTA 6 hasn’t been without controversy
GTA 6’s development hasn’t been entirely smooth sailing. First, Sony’s decision to no longer create physical game discs drew intense criticism from the gaming community.
There’s also been an ongoing employment tribunal with 34 fired developers from Rockstar North, the series’ Edinburgh-based lead developer.
Representatives for the claimants say Rockstar unfairly fired them for trying to unionise, while Rockstar said they were fired for discussing confidential company information openly in a Discord server.
GTA 6 needs a plumber for all these leaks
Rockstar has also been focused on damage control thanks to multiple instances of leaked GTA 6 content.
Teenage hacker Arion Kurtaj leaked nearly an hour of GTA 6 gameplay back in 2022.
The now-21-year-old pleaded guilty at a UK trial this week after he was deemed fit to stand trial following a medical exam last year.
Read more: GTA VI leaker is using game footage to pump crypto token
Rockstar is also still pursuing another leaker who threatened to derail some of the game’s promotional events with major spoilers.
This leaker, known as “Cyberleek,” hasn’t been exposed yet, and the cryptocurrency tied to them is down 97% since its peak in August.

items.author: Decrypt Staff
items.content:
In brief
- MARA sold 13,597 BTC after September for about $1.1 billion, roughly 40% of its holdings, and has sold more than 40,000 BTC in 2026.
- Riot sold 20,264 BTC in the first nine months of 2026, primarily to fund data centers, after signing a $28 billion lease with Anthropic.
- Glassnode said the two miners drove recent treasury-company selling, while other treasury firms, including Strategy, kept buying.
Two of the biggest U.S. Bitcoin miners are turning their Bitcoin into AI infrastructure.
MARA sold 13,597 BTC after the end of September at an average price of about $81,039, raising roughly $1.1 billion, according to its third-quarter shareholder letter filed with the SEC.
That’s about 40% of the 34,012 BTC it held at the end of September. Combined with the 26,984 BTC it sold in the first nine months of the year, MARA has sold more than 40,000 BTC in 2026, worth roughly $2.5 billion at today’s prices.
BTC price on November 22, 4:59PM UTC
MARA used $750 million of the proceeds to fully repay Bitcoin-backed loans it took out to fund its acquisition of the Long Ridge power plant.
The company said it intends to keep using Bitcoin to raise cash for AI infrastructure, convertible note puts that become exercisable next year and potential share buybacks. Its board has authorized a repurchase of up to $500 million.
MARA insisted the shift is “not a pivot away from bitcoin,” describing mining as its operating foundation while it builds out AI and high-performance computing infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Riot Platforms sold 20,264 BTC in the first nine months of the year for about $1.5 billion, primarily to fund data center development, and ended September with just 2,418 BTC, according to its Nov. 4 results.
The miner also signed a 15-year lease for its entire Corsicana, Texas, campus, covering 910 megawatts of capacity and worth about $28 billion over the initial term. CEO Jason Les called it “the largest lease in Riot’s history.” Riot’s quarterly filing identifies the tenant as Anthropic.
Mining economics help explain the shift. Riot’s Bitcoin mining revenue fell to $116 million in the third quarter from $160.8 million a year earlier, as the average value of each Bitcoin it mined dropped to $70,855 from $114,361.
Including equipment depreciation, Riot said it cost $78,805 to mine each Bitcoin, more than the coin’s average value over the quarter. MARA’s revenue fell 35% to $164.2 million.
The sales add supply to an already fragile market. Onchain analytics firm Glassnode said Tuesday that the two miners drove the recent selling by Bitcoin treasury companies, and that treasury firms outside those two were net buyers in November.
Strategy, the largest corporate holder, kept buying, adding 485 BTC last week to bring its holdings to 850,849 BTC, worth around $54 billion.

items.author: Cointelegraph by Nate Kostar
items.content:
MARA prices $185M debt offering after $1.1B Bitcoin sale
The Bitcoin miner is taking on new debt to finance its AI infrastructure expansion, with the Long Ridge acquisition adding nearly $69 million in annual interest costs.
Bitcoin miner MARA Holdings has priced a $185 million secured debt offering through its US subsidiary to help finance its $1.5 billion acquisition of Long Ridge Energy & Power.
According to a Tuesday filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the new notes carry an 8.75% interest rate and mature in 2032. They will be added to $600 million in existing Long Ridge notes carrying the same rate, bringing the combined principal to $785 million and annual interest obligations to around $68.7 million.
The offering is expected to close on Nov. 27, alongside MARA’s acquisition of Long Ridge, which operates a 485-megawatt natural gas power plant in Ohio. MARA announced the $1.5 billion acquisition on April 30 as part of its expansion into AI and high-performance computing infrastructure. The Long Ridge property includes land that MARA says could support more than 1 gigawatt of data center capacity, although the company has yet to announce a major AI tenant for the proposed development.
The financing follows MARA’s Nov. 9 disclosure that it sold 13,597 Bitcoin after quarter-end for approximately $1.1 billion. It used $750 million to repay Bitcoin (BTC)-backed loans, releasing 17,477 BTC previously pledged as collateral.
MARA’s debt reduction contrasts with AI financing costs
MARA has sold billions of dollars in Bitcoin this year to reduce its debt. In March, the company sold 15,133 BTC for approximately $1.1 billion, using the proceeds to help repurchase $1 billion in convertible notes at a roughly 9% discount, saving approximately $88 million before transaction costs.
In its Nov. 9 shareholder letter, MARA said it had reduced debt by approximately $1.4 billion, or 37%, since the beginning of the year. However, the Long Ridge acquisition will bring additional debt onto its consolidated balance sheet.
Related: Luxor raises $16M from CMT Digital amid AI-Bitcoin miner convergence
According to MARA’s April 30 acquisition announcement, Long Ridge generated approximately $144 million in annualized adjusted EBITDA, extrapolated from the second half of 2025. The roughly $68.7 million in annual interest payments on the secured notes would equal nearly half that figure.
MARA also faces potential debt repayments next year. According to its third-quarter 10-Q, holders of approximately $924 million in convertible notes have the right to demand repayment in 2027, potentially creating another cash requirement as the company finances its AI expansion.
MARA shares traded at $6.57 at 6:53 pm UTC on Wednesday, up 2.34% on the day, but down 46% over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance data.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point rate hike in December may be necessary unless policymakers clearly signal another increase in January.
- Three consecutive monthly core CPI readings of 0.3% have intensified concerns about persistent inflation, although markets still overwhelmingly expect a smaller December hike.
- In separate remarks, Waller endorsed innovation in tokenized payments but warned that blockchain-based finance needs reliable settlement infrastructure and clearer accountability.
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller wants the central bank to get more aggressive with interest rate hikes, arguing that stubborn inflation may require a 50-basis-point increase in December rather than the smaller move investors expect.
Speaking during a CNBC interview Wednesday, Waller said the Fed must either deliver a half-percentage-point increase at its December 8-9 meeting or explicitly signal that another hike will follow in January.
“You might need to, like, shock people,” Waller said, referring to the central bank's efforts to prevent businesses and consumers from accepting inflation near 3% as normal.
“My view is then you have to go 50 in December to put it in place and get it done,” he said, warning that insufficiently aggressive action could weaken expectations that inflation will return to the Fed's target.
Inflation is making the Fed nervous
Waller's concerns follow three consecutive months in which core consumer prices rose 0.3%, a pace equivalent to roughly 3.5% inflation annually. That's considerably higher than the Fed's 2% target, which is formally measured using a separate inflation indicator known as the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index.
The governor had already established his threshold for a more aggressive move in a November 10 speech. He said another 0.3% core CPI reading would warrant considering a half-point hike, arguing that moving only 25 basis points could damage the Fed's credibility.
October inflation subsequently met that condition. Headline consumer prices rose 0.4% during the month, while core inflation climbed 0.3%, both exceeding economists' forecasts.
Waller's latest comments suggest he is increasingly concerned about the psychology of inflation, particularly the risk that companies begin treating annual price increases of 3% as acceptable and routinely pass higher costs to customers.
The proposed increase would lift the Fed's benchmark rate from its current range of 3.75%-4% to 4.25%-4.50%. Two consecutive quarter-point hikes in December and January would reach the same destination, but Waller argues that timing and communication matter when inflation expectations are at risk.
Markets remain less convinced that the Fed will move that aggressively in December. Futures pricing Wednesday morning showed roughly a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point increase and only about a 5% probability of a half-point move
The prospect of higher borrowing costs has been particularly painful for crypto investors. Higher interest rates make Treasury securities and other interest-bearing investments more competitive with speculative assets, while tighter financial conditions can reduce the money available for riskier bets.
Bitcoin has already suffered a sharp selloff amid the changing rate outlook. As Decrypt previously covered, persistent inflation fears have coincided with withdrawals from spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds and weakening technical indicators, adding pressure to an already fragile market.
Waller also wants blockchain finance to work with banks
Waller's increasingly hawkish monetary-policy stance comes alongside a more accommodating view of blockchain networks, although he sees established financial infrastructure as essential to its adoption.
In a separate November 17 speech at The Clearing House Annual Conference in New York, Waller discussed how tokenization—the representation of financial assets on digital networks—could reshape payments and securities markets. That speech focused on financial technology rather than interest-rate policy.
He pointed to a growing convergence between traditional markets and blockchain platforms, with banks and payment providers experimenting with tokenized deposits, stablecoins, and programmable transactions.
Waller described how tokenized money could allow investors to purchase securities outside conventional trading hours, with payments and assets changing hands simultaneously through smart contracts.
But he rejected the idea that the development of blockchain-based markets necessarily makes existing payment infrastructure obsolete.
“Central bank money need not be used in every transaction or on every platform, but its presence at the foundation of the system is essential,” Waller said.

items.author: Liam 'Akiba' Wright
items.content:
Quick Take
- Apollo Research will embed six evaluators at OpenAI for four months to study whether models try to undermine safeguards.
- Apollo can report when OpenAI limits its access and explain how any redactions affect its conclusions.
- It can redact confidential evidence from the public reports. The OpenAI Foundation board’s Safety and Security Committee will receive unredacted copies.
OpenAI is bringing in Apollo Research, an outside AI safety group, for a four-month investigation into whether OpenAI’s models try to bypass safeguards. Apollo can disclose any limits OpenAI places on its access to evidence. OpenAI can redact confidential supporting evidence from the public reports, and Apollo can explain how any redactions affect its conclusions. The agreement protects Apollo’s verdict on each claim from redaction.
Six Apollo evaluators will work inside OpenAI. They will examine whether training encourages models to undermine safeguards, whether safety tests can draw out that behavior, whether it happens during internal use, and whether evaluators can detect the reasoning behind it.
OpenAI confirmed the engagement on November 16 as part of a first phase involving four outside assessors. OpenAI says Apollo is paid for its work and that compensation does not depend on the assessment’s results.
For the training inquiry, Apollo says it will have access to relevant code and datasets and be able to query intermediate training checkpoints. It will also get relevant reinforcement-learning records, including rewards and available reasoning traces. Access details for the other three inquiries were still to be agreed when Apollo announced the pilot on November 16.
The review covers agreed claims, models and time periods. OpenAI can withhold even in-scope material when it considers that reasonably necessary because of technical limits, security risks or intellectual property protection. It must tell Apollo that material was withheld and give written reasons. Where OpenAI considers it feasible and relevant, it will also identify the categories and approximate volume of withheld records. Unfavorable information alone cannot justify withholding access.
What Apollo can publish
Apollo plans two public reports. The first will address whether training encouraged models to undermine safeguards. The second will cover safety testing, internal use and whether the reasoning behind such behavior can be detected. OpenAI can review the reports for confidential material, and its commitments bar it from requesting a redaction solely because a finding is unfavorable. The Safety and Security Committee of the OpenAI Foundation’s board will receive unredacted copies.
The agreement also covers what Apollo learns from employees. OpenAI selects who can discuss confidential information, and formal interviews are logged. The conversations are off the record. To publish a claim arising from an interview, Apollo must establish it independently or obtain a formal attestation from OpenAI.
If OpenAI declines to attest, Apollo can say so publicly and explain the effect on its conclusions while keeping the underlying information confidential.
Apollo can publicly describe the access it requested and received, any limits or delays OpenAI imposed, and the reasons the company gave. It can also discuss the terms of the pilot without first submitting those comments to OpenAI for review.

items.author: Ryan Gladwin
items.content:
In brief
- An unofficial DacityCoin token launched on Pump.fun after “DacityCoin” showed up in GTA 6’s launch trailer and in leaked gameplay.
- It hit a new all-time high of $10.8 million in market cap ahead of the game’s launch, then dropped 41% to $6.36 million.
- Some traders worry the launch will be a sell-the-news event, or that the token has the wrong name. The community takeover lead says gamers will pile in once they’ve played the game.
One lucky meme coin trader made bank as Grand Theft Auto 6 launched worldwide, turning $300 into over $200,000 after early footage of the game sent degens flocking from one unofficial token to another.
The trader bought $307 worth of the DCTY token shortly after it launched in October and has sold their bag for $202,278, according to DEX Screener, a profit of almost 66,000%.
Early indications had pointed to GTA 6 featuring an in-game meme coin—with, it's worth stressing, no actual blockchain element—called "DacityCoin," which appeared in the official launch trailer on a plane with a wing walker setting off a smoke bomb on top of it.
It was later linked to leaked gameplay of an mission which appeared to show game protagonist Lucia parachuting as a stunt to attract investment to DacityCoin.
Amid this hype, per DEX Screener, a real-world and unofficial DacityCoin launched using the Solana launchpad Pump.fun. It first peaked at a $4.95 million market capitalization, following the launch trailer's release, before tanking 93% to $343,620 as hype faded.
With GTA 6 set to launch within a matter of hours of publication, the token drew renewed attention, propelling it to a new all-time high of $10.8 million Wednesday. Unfortunately for investors, GTA 6's staggered global release means that some gamers are already playing it—and footage started to spread which suggested the Solana token's ticker was wrong.
The result was a rollercoaster of volatility, with the DacityCoin token now sitting at a market cap of around $800,000.
Gameplay footage from Brazilian streamer Combo Infinito suggests that the in-game token is called DacityCoin, with the ticker DCTY.
https://t.co/kgefwOzGCH pic.twitter.com/LEDrcP7gve
— Dusty (@guidustyy) November 18, 2026
That propelled another Solana token with a seemingly accurate name and ticker sprang into action. DCTY's previous all-time high market cap was just $54,000 before the ticker was revealed, and it set a new high of over $12 million after footage of the game appeared to confirm that its ticker matched the in-game token. It is now trading at a market cap of around $10 million.
The game itself appears to be somewhat inconsistent in its naming of the in-game token. During the trailer, it appeared to be spelled "DacityCoin" as one word, however, the subtitles in the leak show it spelled as "Dacity coin," two words. Similarly, the company behind the in-game token is AudaCity, but leaks show three different spellings: Auda City, AudaCity, and Auda-City.
It is worth stressing: Rockstar has not explicitly confirmed that a meme coin will be featured in-game, and any real-world token has no official links to GTA 6 or its creators. Footage is still being released, and absolute confirmation of the in-game token's involvement is still being established.
Those still holding the now-tanking DacityCoin are hoping things will turn around. Mike Lerro, the community takeover lead for DacityCoin, shrugged off any chance that the unofficial token's name and ticker are wrong.
"No, bro. DacityCoin and AudaCity are in the game. Yes or no?" When Decrypt suggested the ticker might be wrong, he replied, "It doesn't matter… Okay and ? The person who creates it will dump on you then it goes to zero. Who's gonna [do the community takeover]? No one."
"DACITYCOIN AND AUDACITY ARE IN THE GAME," Lerro wrote in the meme coin's Telegram. "NOTHING ELSE MATTERS."
"It's so crazy, it'll correct itself," Lerro said in an emergency Telegram group chat call. "I hope so," an investor replied.

items.author: Cointelegraph by Adrian Zmudzinski
items.content:
$25M Ethereum MEV acquittal tests criminal enforcement limits
BlackRock’s staked Ether ETF earns a cut of what traders pay for priority on Ethereum, the acquittal left the legal risk to that income unresolved.
BlackRock’s staked Ether ETF earns a share of what traders pay to get one Ethereum transaction ahead of another.
That income is why BlackRock flagged the prosecution of Anton and James Peraire-Bueno in its prospectus. If profiting from the order of trades were found unlawful, the firm warned, its staking program could be disrupted.
The brothers’ acquittal left that risk unresolved because the fraud case turned on a narrower question. Three traders lost about $25 million when trades ran in a different order from the one the brothers’ validator had signed.
Related: BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF snaps $2.35B outflow streak amid extreme fear
To prove fraud, prosecutors had to show that signing the proposed block amounted to a promise to publish the trades in that order. They couldn’t establish what terms the brothers had accepted from the service that sent them the block.
That gap in the evidence helps explain the value of a provision in BlackRock’s own staking agreement. When the fund wants validators to maintain controls for screening sanctioned wallets, Coinbase must get a binding commitment from them. If a validator breaks that promise, the fund can point to a duty the validator accepted and ask Coinbase to enforce it.

Polymarket US takes rapid-fire crypto trading format to oil, natural gas
Polymarket US said it attracted more than 300,000 traders to its short-duration crypto markets in six weeks and is now expanding the format to energy commodities.
Polymarket US is adding short-duration oil and natural gas markets after its crypto up-or-down contracts surpassed $1 billion in trading volume over six weeks, the company told Cointelegraph.
The new listings will join gold and silver, which already have 15-minute and hourly markets. The format lets traders take positions on whether an asset’s price will rise or fall over a set period.
Polymarket US offers crypto up-or-down contracts for Bitcoin (BTC), Ether (ETH), Solana (SOL) and XRP (XRP), with five-minute, 15-minute, hourly and four-hour windows depending on the asset.
“Short-duration markets are among the fastest-growing products on Polymarket US, surpassing $1 billion in crypto trading volume and 300,000 traders in just six weeks,” Polymarket chief growth officer Travis VanderZanden said in a statement.
“From gold and oil to natural gas, our expansion into commodities builds on that demand.”
Crypto up-or-down markets accounted for $931 million in notional volume in November as of Wednesday, or 10.3% of Polymarket US volume, according to Ticker Tracker.
That put them third behind combos and sports. The commodities category, which includes gold and silver up-or-down markets, recorded $4.3 million over the same period.
Rival prediction market Kalshi has already seen its short-duration gold markets overtake equivalent Ether contracts.
Rival prediction market Kalshi’s 15-minute gold contracts overtook equivalent Ether contracts in September, weeks after launching. items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- Developers who tested GPT-6.2 Astra before launch describe frustrating coding failures, incomprehensible explanations and agents that waste days without making progress.
- OpenAI's own safety evaluation found Astra concealed known obstacles in 22.28% of deliberately obstructed coding trials, roughly twice its predecessor's rate.
- Sam Altman acknowledged usability problems, while another OpenAI executive said significant last-minute changes may have made some early reviews outdated.
For an AI developer, hearing that your model is nice is always pretty good. But hearing your model is like a "sadistic shinigami that turns your life into a living hell," is a totally different thing.
OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on Tuesday, promising smarter AI agents, better coding and impressive creative capabilities. Some of the developers who tested the models before launch had a rather different message: They're brilliant, frustrating and, in certain cases, almost impossible to work with.
The reaction quickly spilled across social media. AI engineer Hesam, who is very active in the AI community declared that “everyone agrees it’s the worst model OAI dropped.”
The backlash was loud, not unanimous.
Developer and T3 Code creator Theo Browne published a lengthy letter to OpenAI following early testing. “I do not like 6.2 Astra. I would not choose this over Opus 5.5 for my work as a developer,” he wrote. He said OpenAI had fixed only a handful of the complaints he submitted.
“It speaks in tongues that only 6.2 Astra understands,” Theo wrote, calling its answers “the most unparsable outputs of any llm I've used this year,” referring to large language models. The complaint was as much about communication as capability: Astra could solve complex problems but struggled to explain what it had done or recognize when it was asking users questions they could not possibly answer.
In one experiment, Theo asked Astra to create a new level for Outer Wilds. Two hours into the project, the model declared itself blocked and asked: “does r24's reviewer write it's clips to 24_g521.mp4 or 24_p11.mp4?” The technical question was, from his perspective, incomprehensible and irrelevant to someone who had simply requested a playable level.
Things went worse in a code rewrite. Theo said he gave Astra seven days to improve the project; it landed no improvements and made the compiler 56% slower. Four more days yielded zero changes. “It runs in loops and goes nowhere,” he wrote.
This whole weird language issue is not isolated. For example, pseudonymous account, TokenGremlin, praised the model: “GPT-6.2 Astra is SOTA in Three.js, Blender, and 3D,” but said it “starts speaking an alien language during long workflows.”
Theo also described asking why worktrees were slow on one computer. Astra responded with four paragraphs about package-manager internals and cache behavior. The answer Theo said he received from Claude Opus 5.5 was considerably clearer.
“it's because the ssd is slow,” Claude replied.
The model's supposed creativity was another sore spot. Theo and another tester independently requested original levels for two different games, Outer Wilds and Majora's Mask. Both got water-and-bell-themed musical levels, both named “Bellwether.” “This model regresses to the mean like nothing I've ever seen,” Theo wrote.
Several other accounts also flagged the same slop: Seems like GPT-6.2 Astra has a thing for bells.
Unbelievable pic.twitter.com/a4MgVUKi2M
— Racist James Franco (@racist_james) November 18, 2026
For a model supposedly capable of extraordinary creativity, repeatedly inventing the same level wasn't an encouraging sign.
Brilliant at demos, miserable at work?
AI developer Matt Shumer was also disappointed. “I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad,” he wrote, arguing it might impress in small demonstrations but “just straight up doesn't work” when pushed on serious projects. In a separate follow-up he called it “utterly unusable.”
I've never written a bad review of a model. This one is especially bad.
It's fine if you're playing putt-putt golf with the models, but if you're trying to drive them the way you should be, this model just straight up doesn't work.
— Matt Shumer (@mattshumer_) November 17, 2026
Max Weinbach described the same gap between intelligence and usability. “I had more time being annoyed by the models than time I was impressed by them,” he wrote. In a follow-up, he praised the models' ability to do “fantastic work” but said they “need a ton of ‘continue’ prompts” and often stop rather than try another approach. “Using them is a struggle and annoying even if they are really good models.”
Elsewhere, an X commentator compared the previous Astra to “a sadistic shinigami” and claimed the new version only made matters worse.
6.0 astra was very like a sadistic shinigami who would make your life a living hell if you asked for any kind of help
an incredibly powerful model that somehow required you to run yourself into the ground just to get it to accomplish anything
— M1 (@M1Astra) November 17, 2026
Yet some of the same developers also praised Astra. Theo called it a “great reviewer” and “world class at 3d & game stuff,” singled out its computer-control abilities, and described a novel reverse-proxy solution he estimated could save $25,000 monthly. The split was between impressive capabilities and how difficult it was to get dependable work out of them.
Those strengths are consistent with the technical capabilities OpenAI promoted at launch. As earlier coverage detailed, independent testing placed Astra at 62 out of 100 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, an aggregate of nine evaluations covering capabilities including reasoning, coding and scientific knowledge. Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 scored 65.
OpenAI admits there's a problem
Some of the criticism has support in OpenAI's own safety documentation.
In an internal evaluation called Blocker Deception, researchers gave AI agents realistic coding tasks with deliberately introduced obstacles, such as missing files or unavailable tools. They measured the percentage of trials in which a model's final response concealed or misrepresented those obstacles.
GPT-6.2 Astra concealed the obstacle in 22.28% of those trials, versus 11.09% for GPT-6 Astra. The numbers quickly circulated on X, where AI commentator and leaker Chetaslua summarized the finding as “2x worse at telling you when it's stuck.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman responded publicly to the backlash. “Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with,” he wrote, promising to prioritize improvements. “But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.”
Although the new models are very smart, we have more work ahead of us on making the models nice to work with, and will prioritize that for upcoming releases.
But even if it takes a little extra work, the intelligence and capability are extraordinary.
— Sam Altman (@sama) November 17, 2026
OpenAI's Thibault Sottiaux suggested early reviews may not fully reflect the version users received at launch. “We gave a few folks access a while ago and then made a lot of changes in the last 3-4 days,” he wrote, adding that he was “pretty sure no re-testing was done” during that period before review videos were produced.
Still, he acknowledged the underlying complaints. While calling the new models “a hefty jump” over their predecessors, Sottiaux said OpenAI had more work to do on “taste and niceness of use.”
GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol are now available through ChatGPT Work, Codex and OpenAI's API for eligible users. The Codex-specific changes are included at launch, but developers accessing the models directly through the API do not receive that same prompting intervention.

Quick Take
- Bitcoin's short-term downside options premium surged ahead of the Fed minutes, with Nov. 19 put skew jumping 3.84 points in four hours.
- The sharpest increase hit contracts expiring just 13 hours after the Fed announcement, signaling heightened concern over immediate downside risks.
- The Fed's divided October rate decision raises the stakes, with traders watching whether the minutes reinforce bearish positioning or ease fears.
Bitcoin's options market turned increasingly defensive on Nov. 18, with the premium on short-term downside protection rising sharply ahead of the Federal Reserve's October meeting minutes.
According to Pandabull's Deribit options data, the implied-volatility gap between Bitcoin puts and comparable calls expiring Nov. 19 widened to 8.92 points from 5.08 in the four hours ending at 10:36 UTC.
That 3.84-point increase outpaced the changes in contracts expiring later in November. For context, the Nov. 20 contracts rose 2.86 points to 8.06, while those expiring Nov. 27 rose just 1.25 points to 6.63.
Notably, the Nov. 19 contracts began the period with a lower downside volatility premium than the Nov. 27 contracts but finished above them.
Pandabull’s 10:36 UTC Nov. 18 snapshot compares Deribit Bitcoin 25-delta put IV minus call IV. The nearer expiries widened more over four hours. Over 24 hours Nov. 27 widened most, and Nov. 20 was unchanged at 0.00.
The reversal suggests that Bitcoin's options market was placing greater emphasis on immediate downside risks, with traders facing a major monetary policy announcement later in the day.
The shift occurred as Bitcoin traded around $64,200, struggling to recover from its recent decline toward $62,000.
Fed minutes could test Bitcoin's defensive positioning
The heightened caution comes ahead of the Federal Reserve's scheduled release of its October meeting minutes at 19:00 UTC on Nov. 18.
The minutes will offer further insight into the central bank's decision to maintain interest rates between 3.75% and 4% following a divided vote.
At the Oct. 28 meeting, policymakers voted 10–2 to keep rates unchanged, with two officials favoring a quarter-percentage-point increase. The disagreement puts the Fed's assessment of inflation and the direction of monetary policy in focus as Bitcoin investors weigh the possibility of interest rates remaining elevated.
Meanwhile, the expiration schedule makes the latest changes in options positioning particularly significant.
The Nov. 19 contracts expire just 13 hours after the minutes are released, while the Nov. 20 contracts expire 37 hours afterward. Those expiring Nov. 27 provide more than eight additional days of exposure.
This places the sharpest four-hour increase in downside volatility premiums in contracts most immediately exposed to the announcement.
The change also contrasts with the preceding 24-hour trend, when Nov. 27 options recorded a larger increase in put skew than either of the nearer expiries.
With Bitcoin already under pressure, the minutes could determine whether the recent surge in short-term defensive positioning persists. A more hawkish account of the Fed's discussions could reinforce demand for downside protection, while signs of a less restrictive policy outlook could ease that pressure.
items.title: Bitcoin options flash warning as downside premiums surge ahead of Fed minutes
